speechtext:
I beg leave to make a statement
in reference to the recent judgment of the Court of Appeal for Manitoba in the case of the King vs. the Manitoba Grain Company.
The Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada have concluded, upon the advice of their counsel, to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada from the recent judgment of the Court of Appeal for Manitoba in the case of The King vs. The Manitoba Grain Company, whereby it was held that section 215 of the Canada Grain Act is ultra vires of the Parliament of Canada, and pending the review of that decision

Supply-Railways
by the ultimate tribunal it is not the intention of the Government to introduce any measure to amend the Canada Grain Act based upon the view expressed by the Court of Appeal, and the existing provisions will continue to be administered as heretofore. Obviously if these provisions be upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada no amendment will be necessary. If, on the other hand, the judgment of the Court of Appeal be affirmed, the Government will consider the propriety of introducing such further advisable legislation as may be found to be within the scope of the Dominion powers as interpreted by the court.

I did not happen to be in the House yesterday when the railway question was up for consideration, but I was present some weeks ago when the Minister of Railways made a statement in connection with our railways. In that statement, which was carefully prepared and very complete, the minister disclosed a lot of facts bearing on the railway situation, and also announced that it was the intention of the Government to recognize the principle of public ownership with respect to the railways which we have acquired and, in the administration of those railways, to give that principle a fair trial. Yesterday the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell) addressed the House on the railway question and took quite a contrary view, although he too declared that he was favourable to giving public ownership a fair trial. Nevertheless the hon. member told the House frankly

has been so successful in the business of transportation. The Canadian Pacific, through the newspapers of this country and in various other ways, has told this House that we must not go into transportation; and yet the people of Canada, through its Parliament, created the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. That is, the creature says that its creator must not do what it desires to do, but must keep out of the transportation business. When we created the Canadian Pacific and these other railways, we did not create them to say to us that we should not go into transportation if the people saw fit to do so and thought that they could get more efficient service in that way. Therefore, for all these reasons, there is no question about the advantages of public ownership. Under public ownership, you can finance railways better, you can manage them better; you can avail yourself of any system as a complementary system in connection with the railways, and moreover, you have freedom in connection with the railways for all time.
It was said yesterday by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell) that public ownership had never been a success. Has private ownership, company ownership, in this country been a success? Has the Grand Trunk been a success? Has the Canadian Northern been a success? Have hundreds of railway companies in the United States been successful? They have practically all failed, and as I pointed out in this House some time ago, railways in the United States have made confession that they can not go on. Billions of the money of the people of the United States were put into these defaulting railways to carry them through the war, and they cannot go ahead to-day. What is the good of pointing out to us that public ownership is no good, when we know that private ownership, as experienced, in the United States, has been an absolute failure?
What about the Canadian Pacific?

It was subsidized, it was given millions of money and millions of acres of land, by the people of Canada; and it is charging exorbitant rates to-day to the people of Canada. Yes, let the Canadian Pacific make money under these exorbitant rates; but can the service be done for less money and better done by the people, with the men on this railway treated just as well as

they are to-day being treated by the Canadian Pacific? That is the question. Are we going to get a better service and to have the railway better financed? While the Canadian Pacific is an example of the success of private ownership, the more successful the Canadian Pacific becomes, the more likely is it ultimately to be the master of this country. Where is this great success of the Canadian Pacific going to end? Who knows how wealthy the Canadian Pacific is to-day, what millions it has in its strong box which really belong to the people of Canada, and which ought to have been returned to them long ago in the shape of reduced railway charges? That is the point, and not how successful the Canadian Pacific has been in making money. My hon. friend opposite, however, says: See how successful the Canadian Pacific has been in accumulating huge reserves in its treasury. As I said a moment ago, where is this growth of the Canadian Pacific going to end? Do my hon. friends, who speak so much in favour of the Canadian Pacific and who are constantly quoting it, know that there is a very peculiar thing in connection with that railway, and that is the creation of a voting trust which will become stronger if it is permitted to grow? How many members of this House at present know that the Canadian Pacific, which is exalted before our eyes as the most successful example of private ownership, has a voting trust; that only two members of the board retire each year, and that the concluding words of the annual report state that " Messrs. So-and-so " -two members-" retire from the board this year and are subject to re-election?" But to-day even the shareholders cannot exercise their freedom in connection with the Canadian Pacific and change if a new condition arises. Let me tell the House and the country that this voting trust in connection with the Canadian Pacific is the greatest menace that we have in Canada, because now the interests before the people-
Why cannot the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific elect their own directors? I do not think there is anything in their charter to prevent them from doing so.

Only two
directors can be elected each year. The Canadian Pacific has created this permanent voting trust, which was not the rule

Supply-Railways
in the past, and this shows us that the Canadian Pacific is gradually getting stronger. It is an outstanding fact in connection with railway administration that, while it is the people who use the roads and the shareholders who own the roads, it is getting to be more and more these little inside trusts that control even the shareholders and their property, and the shareholders have not the freedom which they used to have. Gradually the railways have come into the hands of little cliques on the inside who control them and who keep themselves in power by these voting trusts. That is the situation to-day in connection with the Canadian Pacific. In the old days a fresh board of directors could be elected at the annual meeting.
What control have the people of Canada over the election of directors of the Canadian National Railways at present?

I hope we have a responsible government in power to do that work. My hon. friend apparently does not believe in responsible government. The shareholders of the Canadian Pacific are entitled to have their directors come under review every year, instead of two being retired each year so that the trust can continue. This creation of voting trusts is getting to be more and more the menace of financial institutions. The richest corporation outside of railways is a certain mining company which has passed into the perpetual control of the people at present in control of it, because, by means of this voting trust, the control can be handed down in perpetuity to their descendants. This matter of voting trusts is the menace of business and of politics in this country.

Will my right hon.
friend allow me a question?
I am not your "right honourable" friend.
Well, my honourable friend," then. Do the shareholders in this company, which the hon. gentleman speaks about, control by a majority, just as in the case of other concerns?

I am not
going to go into the details of the matter, but I know that the system in connection with this company has worked very satisfactorily. It was decided that the management of the company could be entailed, like property, and an entailed administration in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway, which was created by the people, is being developed in Montreal. I will now proceed to give my experiences in connection with public ownership. The member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell) yesterday referred to some things that had happened in my province. Let me tell the committee what has been done in Ontario in regard to public ownership.
The Hydro Electric?

Yes, the
Hydro Electric; and if my hon. friend's province had an Adam Beck they would have a great future ahead of them. I should like my hon. friends from Quebec to visit the city of Toronto, where they would see the finest street railway in America, and one that is owned by the people. It is just as good as the street railway in Montreal, and the people own it, whereas the people of Montreal do not own the street railway there. The people of Toronto can reduce the fare the moment conditions will permit, and they intend to do so. The net rate is at present six cents.
Is the service good?

Yes, and it is being improved as expeditiously as possible. I might observe that the new cars that are being secured will be made in the province of Quebec. Now, I state without fear of contradiction that the best street railway in America to-day is that which is owned by the people of Toronto. The fares are reasonably cheap considering the effects of the war, and they can, and will be reduced whenever it is at all practicable to reduce them. I would seriously ask the hon. gentlemen to go and observe at first hand the satisfactory operation of this public-owned utility. Electrical energy is distributed more cheaply in Toronto than in any other city of similar size, and the facts amply prove this assertion. The municipalities of Ontario are to-day organizing the greatest system of distribution of electrical energy that will be found anywhere in the world. This power is all to be derived from Niagara, and the entire system is to be owned by the people. The scheme contemplates the distribution of energy to every house in the southern portion of Ontario. The plant is greater than that which is to be found on the Tennessee river, and this
Supply-Railways

system of public ownership applied to the development of power in Ontario will within two years produce at least half a million-I believe a million-horse power annually. At $10 per horse power this will represent an income of at least $5,000,000 a year; and if, as I believe, the power reaches the higher figure, the return will, of course, be $10,000,000. Many of the cities of Ontario own their own street railways and they would not part with them under any consideration. At Windsor on the Ontario side of the Detroit river there is a splendid system of public ownership and the service is splendid. Let me tell hon. gentlemen .who are denouncing public ownership that the city of Detroit has taken over the street railway there, following the example of Toronto and other Canadian cities, while in the western provinces the people have tried public ownership of street railways with success. We are building a great system of public ownership here notwithstanding a certain degree of opposition, and in the United States the President and his party are now committed tc a considerable scheme of publicly controlled development of electrical energy wherever it is possible in connection with the railways, in order to provide cheap transportation.
If public ownership is such a good thing how does my hon. friend explain the fact that the American government turned over the railways to their private owners?

The fact is that the American railways could not serve the nation in time of war. They had absolutely fallen down. They had been so exploited by private ownership, the directors and managers being connected with different companies on the side, that the treasuries of the railroads were nearly depleted. They were nearly ruined-and I use the word advisedly-that they could not render the service required of them by the nation during the war, and the government had to take them over and administer them. They have given them back-
Why?

Well, things were in such a bad shape that there had to be a readjustment, and in the meantime they have been handed back to the private owners. But the government will eventually have to take them over again. They have spent millions of dollars on

them, and they will take them over just as we have taken over the railways in this country.

What about Great
Britain?
Mr. MACLEAN York) : Private ownership did not prove successful there, either, during the war. There were twenty systems in that country and the only thing that could be done was to nationalize them. Now, public ownership is sweeping all over the world, and that is what my hon. friends cannot see.

What
about Prance? Have they not handed back the railways to the private owners there?
What about Bulgaria?

Evidently hen. gentlemen are*not serious; they are not dealing with facts. Public ownership has vindicated itself in Europe, in this country, and in Australia, and they are realizing the wisdom of it in the United States. Those who do not see it do not want to see it. There are too many blind men in this House. It may be all right to have a blind
Pig.
No, I am not talking about that. It may be all right to have a blind man, but it is disastrous to have a blind party.
Will you allow me a question? Why do you not come to Quebec and see what effect public management has there?

Well, who is to blame for that but the people of Quebec? That is the thing I am in favour of. When there is mismanagement, if the road is publicly owned it can be rectified, but if the road is privately owned, it cannot be.
If we are to make a success of these railways, the people must have a say in the matter. If the people of Quebec, for instance, have no voice in the matter, how can the railways be made a success?

Well, you have the Government here, with more ministers from Quebec than from any other province. The people must take care of themselves, but you must not deprive them of

Supply-Railways
the right to take care of themselves by handing these franchises over to private companies.

Does the hon. member suggest that the Government should interfere in the management of the National
Railways?

The Minister of Railways says it is the intention of the Government to appoint a board of directors to administer the National Railways. I may say that I am confident that the Government will appoint a good board.
That is not my question. Does the hon. member suggest that the Government should interfere in the management of the National Railways?

Only to the
extent that the minister has mentioned- that the Government get the best possible board to administer the system. The minister is responsible for seeing that that is done.
To whom will that board be responsible?

As is the case in all our public administration, it goes back to the individual voter. But between the voter and the system is the government, and between the government and the system is the board of directors. My hon. friends opposite are fond of preaching the doctrine of, "Trust the people". Do they say that the people cannot be trusted to see that there is a good board of directors?
Would my hon. friend still support public ownership of the railways if the headquarters were transferred to Montreal?

I do not know. Would my hon. friend himself trust Montreal? I attended a meeting of the Railway Committee this morning and I understood there was some doubt about trusting Montreal. Now, these are nice little questions, but they do not interfere with the argument.

Would my hon. friend be in favour of appointing a board of directors the members of which are already directors of companies which manufacture railways cars, locomotives, or steel rails, or operate coal mines, and so on?

No, I would not approve of that. We have heard some intimations from the other side along that
line, from some of the friends of the government. I have not the responsibility of administration of this act, but if I had anything to do with it I would do my share towards seeing that a good board was appointed, and there are good men in Canada who could carry out efficiently the work of such a board. We are just as good as the people of any other country; we have a great many men who are trained in railway matters and who could serve well in this capacity.
What would happen if we gave these railways back, as the Canadian Pacific suggests? Well, it would not be long before Parliament would be asked to vote an enormous sum to put them on their feet. We are not going to do that. We have these roads; let us stand for the deficits until such time as they can be put in shape. We are not going to hand them back to anybody, least of all are we going to hand them to the Canadian Pacific. We will keep them and get good men to administer them.
A great amount of the relief which is afforded in the way of transportation throughout the world is that which the waterways offer. In Europe they have not very good railroads, but they have a great system of waterways. There is not a town in Europe that is not connected with a section of seaboard or with a river; they have constant competition and good service. They have made more of their water transportation than anything else; in this country almost an opposite view is taken. In addition to waterway transportation we have the transportation of the highway. The highway is becoming one of the most aggressive of tjjie competitors of the railroad. Perhaps we shall have a system of transportation in the air before long, but the competitors of the railroad now are the waterways and the highways. Now, there is no doubt that transportation by motor truck and by vessels on our waterway systems will have to be harmonized and brought into co-operation with transportation by rail. The railways do not want to do it; they do not want to avail themselves of the waterways. But the great merit of these various systems is the competition in the way of rates and service which they afford. The advantage of the motor truck is that it transports commodities from door to door, from factory to retailer or consumer, from the mine to wherever the material is required. Therefore in attempting a solution of our transportation problem, we must deal with the

Supply-Railways
question of our waterways and our highways; we must consider all the methods of transportation, and we must harmonize them and bring them into co-operation. We must remember that we not only have to administer these roads, but also we have to see that they give good service.
I come now to the question of motive power for the railways. We have an immense mileage of railroads in this country that have been taken over by the Government, and we have to have motive power for them. The railroads of the United States are up against this same problem of motive power, and the President of the United States has had to come to their relief. He has propounded a great system of water-power development for the haulage of the railway trains of the United States, and the people of the United States are committing themselves to the expenditure of billions of dollars to solve this question of motive power. The railroads over there either own or control a lot of mines to supply the coal required in their operations. So, this problem is up in the United States as well as here, and the only way to solve it is through the development of water-power owned and controlled by the people. There is enough water-power in Canada, in the western rivers, in the rivers of Ontario and Quebec, to provide every railway in this country with motive power. That power cannot be developed in any other way as efficiently and as cheaply as it can under public ownership. There is no way out of the transportation difficulties of America to-day except by electrical energy applied to the railways, and all the railway authorities in the United States insist upon the electrification of their roads, at an enormous cost. I do not know where they are going to get the money, but they can only get cheap water-power as a public-owned proposition, they will never get it cheaply from private-owned concerns. We know how the mine owners exact exorbitant charges from the railway companies of the United States, and they would do the same here if they had the chance. So, we have to go in for the electrification of our railways, .just as the United States are doing. President Harding has accepted that responsibility, and has committed his administration to the principle of the great development of water-power, under public control, for the haulage of the trains of the United States. We in Canada have the railways on our hands, and we intend to keep them and to make them efficient, and we must undertake this duty of electrifying [Mr W. F. Maclean.]
them. We must find water-power for them, and if we do that, we shall be able to give our people a much better system of transportation than they have had in the past.

I believe there are competent men available, and the sooner they are appointed the better it will be for the railways. There has been too much delay in the past, and the Government ought to get busy and appoint the board as soon as possible-the sooner the better so that they can get down and study the great necessities of this country, as outlined yesterday by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). I know why so much opposition is made to public ownership. It is because the people of Canada have got two great railway systems in their hands, and the greatest railway asset in Canada to-day is the Grand Trunk which has passed into the hands of the people. It commands the strategic points all over Canada. The Grand Trunk is stronger to-day in Montreal than the Canadian Pacific. It is strong in the city of Ottawa, and in Toronto it has all the good points, and on the Detroit and Niagara rivers. The same is true of the Canadian Northern and of the Grand Trunk Pacific. We have got all the best points right across the continent through acquiring these railway systems, and they should be linked up into a unified system. When that is done, we shall get lower rates and better service, and we shall be in a position to treat the railway men better than they have ever been treated before. You can unify. The people now have in their hands the business of the transportation of freight and passengers, the express business, the money order business, the telegraph business, and the transfer of mails. It is all right when these are concentrated in the hands of the people. The Canadian Pacific say that we should not be in this business. The Canadian Pacific is in another great combination. The greatest combination in the United States to-day is the American Telegraph and Telephone Company. It controls all the telegraphs and most of the Bell lines all over the
world, and most of the cables all over the world. The Canadian Pacific is in with that combination, and I say it is absolutely necessary in the public interest, not only in Canada, but in the United States and every other modern country, that services associated with transportation should be in the hands of the people such as the telegraph, money order, postal and express business. These should not be in the hands of private corporations. And so I trust that the Minister of Railways will persuade his Government to assume this responsibility. The legislation passed by the previous government, providing for the consolidation of the railways, can be put into effect almost immediately and a good board selected almost at once. If the Government do that, and provide for the consolidation of these roads, you will see the railroads not only paying their operating expenses but beginning to discharge some of the deficits which they have incurred in the past. The prediction I make in connection with the National Railways is that we are going to wipe out these deficits; and it is because the era of public ownership is likely to come, and be a great success that the main opposition to it is encountered to-day. From our experience in the province of Ontario we believe more in public ownership to-day than we ever did. That policy has not fallen down, and there has not been the failure we have seen in the case of the private owned companies. The people did not bring about these deficits met with in the past; they were the result of maladministration and over-building. These railways are to-day in the hands of the people; the government have taken them in charge, and at a very early date they must disclose who are to constitute the board and what measures will be taken to ensure that the consolidation so necessary shall take place at the earliest possible date.

There is no reason why the two systems should not work in co-operation, and, enable passengers to go from one railroad to the other if necessary, and in every way give a better service to the people. The railways of this country will very soon have all they can do, even though that condition does not exist at present, and the

It means a capital outlay of an immense amount-over a billion dollars-imposed on this country; pretty nearly half of the public debt of Canada. The partisans of public ownership in this country may be assigned to two categories. The first comprises those who believe in public ownership as a gospel. The fate of other countries has failed to impress them; nor does our own misfortune move them. The theory sounds good to them, and they hope that facts and figures will some day confirm their belief. This class of worshippers, the Messianic hopeful, is in my opinion getting scarcer every day. But there is another category, much more numerous, who believe in public ownership in their own peculiar way. They do not believe that public ownership can be as successful financially as a private enterprise, they know that it will produce deficits; but they consider the necessity of

retaining the local advantage that it holds for their own portion of territory. In other words, they claim that the railways are a public utility and not a business venture, and that the whole community should control it in order to ensure low freight and passenger rates. Now, some people are asking the question:	What are we to do with the railways? On that point I agree with the remark made by the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) yesterday, that we have too many railway lines in Canada. One who travels to the Pacific coast is struck with the fact that on exceedingly long distances
we have parallel lines traversing wild and unsettled parts of the country in order to link the East and the West, the West and the Coast. Such is the case of the Canadian Northern line from North Bay to Winnipeg, which merely duplicates the Canadian Pacific. Such is the case of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific from Edmonton to Mount Robson junction-in fact, only one of the two is now being used. After a few hours of travel to the south, the Canadian Northern parallels the Canadian Pacific from Kamloops to the Coast. In the last instance, the Canadian Northern being junior to the Canadian Pacific, the line had to be built on the less advantageous slope of the Thompson and Fraser rivers, taking a second choice. It must have been built at tremendous cost, but on account of these circumstances it is decidedly handicapped. In my humble opinion, the transcontinental line from Quebec to Winnipeg and the Grand Trunk Pacific from Edmonton to Prince Rupert have great trade possibilities in the distant future, but I fail to see how the Canadian Northern in the parts that I have mentioned can ever hope but to be operated at a tremendous loss, because it meets no requirements, it merely duplicates a senior line which itself operates at a loss in that part of the country. The case of the transcontinental railways may well be likened to human beings who, we will say, are fed only every two days. The railways have to take a lot of nourishment in the East if they want to avoid starving in the Algoma district, and, again, must overfeed themselves in the West before they cross the Rockies. In my estimation the Canadian Northern should have remained a mere feeder; it should never have attempted either to come East or to reach the Coast.
I believe also that much can be done by the exercise of rigid economy and by increasing immigration. These subjects have already been dealt with, however, and I shall do no more than allude to them. But if we are going to give these railways a trial, the Government is to do its utmost to decrease the deficit, it should not fail to take advantage of any opportunity that offers itself to free the country from that burden.
In conclusion, I admit that the Government may have no other course open to it than that of operating these lines to the best of its ability. Advocates of government ownership may rejoice over the fact that this will constitute a trial of the prin-

ciple that they favour. But, disbelieving, as I do, in that style of administration, I am quite convinced that the result will inevitably be to add many millions to the public debt. Possibly we are not able to avoid that, but we should make it very clear, Mr. Chairman, that, hard as we may try to make the burden lighter for the Canadian taxpayers, we on this side decline all responsibility; that these railways were thrust upon us; that we accept the burden only with the greatest reluctance; that the railways are on the market for the earliest buyer who can give sufficient guarantee of good faith and fair operation; and that the sooner we can dispose of them and return to private ownership the better it will be both for the Government and for the country.

I have only two reasons to offer for rising to intervene in this debate. One is because of the tremendous importance of the subject under discussion, and the other is because of the rather remarkable trend of the debate on this side of the House. It would be very easy, Mr. Chairman, to criticise the policies of former governments which have brought us into our present position with regard to the national railways. That sort of debate, however, is, to my mind, largely a waste of time.	We have arrived
at a certain condition; the facts are as they are, and I do not care to indulge in partisan recriminations which sometimes engage the members.
There are only two alternatives before Parliament. One is to accept our responsibility faithfully to operate the railways as a publicly owned utility in the interests of the people; the other, as has been suggested by my hon. friend who preceded me, is to return the National Railways to private ownership as soon as possible. I may say frankly that I very much prefer the first alternative. I am a believer in the principle of public ownership, and I believe that the railways of Canada, now under our control, can succeed provided that we make an honest and whole-hearted effort to make them successful. If we returned these roads to private ownership, it is my opinion that the ultimate outcome would be their incorporation in the Canadian Pacific Railway system. I think the. people of Canada would consider that a calamity. They would view with alarm any suggestion that any one railway com-
pany, however efficient it may be, should have a monopoly of the railway business of this country.
I know that there are rumours in the corridors and occasionally in the press that there is still another alternative to that of the Canadian Pacific taking over the National Railways, and it is that another private company might be formed which would take over our railways and operate them in competition with the Canadian Pacific. I have not a great deal of faith in that alternative. Even under the most favourable conditions we shall most probably have serious deficits in the operation of the National Railways for some years to come, and I for one question whether a company sufficiently strong financially could be found to bear the strain for the number of years it would be necessary to operate, until they would reach a period of prosperity. I fear that even if the roads did go to a company other than the Canadian Pacific, the final result would be the same, and the Canadian Pacific ultimately would be found in possession.
I believe this also, that if one private railway company came into control of all the railways in Canada, we would no longer receive the efficient service that we now receive from the Canadian Pacific; for, if you remove competition entirely, you remove that incentive to efficiency and service to the public which exists to-day.
Yesterday the hon. member for Marquette delivered what I thought was a most excellent speech on the railway situation. I agreed almost entirely with his views. He said what I would have said, and much better than I could have said it. For that reason it would be out of place for me to reiterate the views he has expressed so exhaustively. Yet, on the other hand, it would be regrettable if there were not at least one member on this side of the House to declare that he believed in the principle of public ownership and had some faith that the National Railways under public management can be made a success if we address ourselves honestly to that task.
The hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell) also delivered a speech yesterday which, in its general tenor, was directly opposed to that of the hon. member for Marquette. With much that the hon. member for St. Antoine said yesterday I was in hearty accord. That the National Railways must secure the very best men possible for the management of the roads I quite agree, and every member of the House

takes the same position. In fact, that goes without saying, unless we deliberately set out to wreck the National Railways, which purpose I do not for one moment attribute to any one. The most important official that we have to find is, of course, the chairman of the new railway board which is to be constituted, and which will be named by the Minister of Railways, I hope, at a very early date. It may be that such a man may be found in Canada. It is even conceivable that he may be a man who has not been entirely and exclusively associated with railways. But we do need a man of first-class and proven executive ability. We need a man of strict integrity, and one who has the confidence of the people of Canada as well as the confidence of the members of Parliament. We need a man who has himself faith in the public ownership principle, and who has, something of a passion for public service. His will be a great task, but if it is a great task for the chairman of the new board and a tremendous responsibility, I say that it is also a tremendous opportunity and a splendid challenge for some big man in this country to perform perhaps the greatest service that is possible for the people of Canada to-day.
The hon. member for St. Antoine also spoke of the necessity for a proper accounting with regard to our national railways. I do not know if he has information with which I am not familiar. It may be that the books of the National Railways are not kept in a proper manner. It may be that we have entered as assets upon these books some things which have no longer any existence in fact, such, for example, the abandoned road-beds as referred to by the hon. member for Marquette yesterday. If that is the case, they should certainly be written off, so that the books of the National Railways will show the facts and the assets as they are. It may also be that there has been a practice, as there very frequently is, not only in connection with publicly owned utilities but with private corporations as well, of charging up to capital what is properly chargeable to profit and loss account. If that has been done, I think the matter should be investigated, and corrected.
The hon. member for Marquette said yesterday, as he did also in last year's debate, that there should be a revaluation of the National Railways. I agree with that. It is good business practice to have your books show exactly what your assets are, and not to carry any that are fictitious or over-valued. I would, however, say this: If he implies by What he said yesterday that certain assets should be wiped off the books, and in connection with that, that the annual charges based upon those assets and covered by bonds should no longer be chargeable to the railways but to the Consolidated Fund, that may be good practice; I have no fault to find with that. But the public should thoroughly understand that that in itself will not lighten the burden of deficits on the people. It may have a good effect in this way. The board of management will be encouraged by the fact that they are relieved of some of the present heavy fixed charges, although as a matter of fact the charges are merely transferred to consolidated revenue account and in no wise relieve the Canadian tax-payers. I have said that in the statements of the hon. member for St. Antoine to which I have referred, I quite agree with him. But when he declares himself opposed in principle to public ownership and expresses lack of faith in the ultimate success of the National Railways, I must disassociate myself from those sentiments. I have a good deal of regard for the hon. member for St. Antoine. He comes to this House from a most important office in the province of Quebec, with a reputation for efficiency and as a successful executive in the government of that province.
And so I say I regard his opinion as worthy of consideration. I do not question his right to take the attitude that he does, although I will say frankly, and without any thought of giving offence to anyone, that I doubt very much-considering all the circumstances and the fact that we now have the railways and have declared that we are going to give them a fair chance to succeed-I doubt very much the judgment of those who to-day declare that they do not believe we can be successful in the management and operation of these roads. The expression of such sentiments does not make for success in our great undertaking.
Now that we have these railways I agree in part with the hon. member (Mr. Rinfret) who has just spoken, that it becomes our duty-at least the duty of those of us who believe in public ownership-under all the circumstances as so far disclosed in the debate, to declare our faith in the principle and in the prospect of success. I admit frankly, Sir, that I listened with consider-

able regret to the remarks derogatory to public ownership and the operation of national railways that have been made. When a man goes into a fight and declares beforehand that he knows he is going to be beaten, he has lost the fight before he starts. I know very well that many hon. members on both sides of the House disagree with me on the matter of public ownership. One of my friends who generally sits to my right, would give the railways away for the sum of one dollar, but I hope he was not serious in that observation. It is true that in the previous parliament there were probably not more than half a dozen members who honestly believed in public ownership and operation of railways. If there was more than that number they never declared their belief in this chamber. And I am sometimes humiliated as a Canadian to have my fellow members, and the press of this country, say that they do not believe there are men in Canada who can run our railways as well as private corporations can. Sir, I believe there are men in this country who have the ability and the public spirit to administer this great trust in the interests of the Canadian people. To believe less than that is, in my opinion, to display an attitude unworthy of the representatives of a people who have shown in the past that they can rise to any emergency in the interest of Canada.
In matters such as this we judge, or ought to judge, by experience, if experience is available. I am very sorry that the experience of the hon. member for St. Antoine has been so unfortunate as regards the matter of public ownership and operation of public utilities. He told us yesterday that in his experience of municipal affairs in Quebec he did not know of a single instance where public ownership had been successful. Now, I hope he did not have th^ opportunity, or necessity, of dealing with very many instances, because I would be sorry to know that in the province of Quebec they cannot make public ownership a success. I do not care to make comparisons but I will say that I can tell a brighter story for the province of Ontario, and especially for western Ontario of which I know something. Dozens of municipalities in that province have administered their public utilities with entire success. They have operated their gas plants, their electric light plants, their waterworks, and in many instances their electric railways, with entire success and to the satisfaction of the people. In my own city of Kitchener

-where the population is 23,000, but combined with that of Waterloo reaches a total of 29,000 or 30,000 people-we have operated all these utilities. We have operated our street railway and it has been successful. There has never been the slightest accusation that into the operation of that road, or in the employment of men, favouritism, or local politics, or anything of the kind, has ever entered. We have had business men with sense of public duty who have administered these utilities without any remuneration whatever; and so far as our railway is concerned, if I might particularize in that one case, it has been operated with a profit each year. It has taken care of its debentures both as to principal and interest, as they matured, out of the revenue. It has, almost each year, paid into the municipal treasury an amount, larger or smaller, towards the reduction of taxes; and it has done that with a five cent fare. From the operation of public utilities in the municipalities, the province itself has advanced into a larger field. We have there what is known as the Hydro Electric system. I want to say this-and I do so with a full knowledge of what I am saying-that the Hydro Electric in the province of Ontario, despite the reports and propaganda to the contrary, that has been carried on in certain parts of Canada, has been an undoubted success. I am not now referring to certain other suggestions with regard to the proposed construction of radial railways; I am now referring to the distribution of hydro-electric energy for the purpose of power, and electric lighting throughout the municipalities of western Ontario. To-day we pay only a fraction of the cost that was paid under private ownership for electric current. We know it is a success by having recourse to the same method that Sir Wilfrid Laurier invited the people of Canada to use in order to test the success of his policy when he said, "We do not have to tell you that there is prosperity in Canada, you feel it in your pockets." That is exactly how we measure the benefits of the Hydro-Electric in western Ontario. Now I admit that that in itself is not an absolute proof that we can do the same in the national field and make public ownership and operation of railways a success; but it is at least evidence tending in that direction and encouraging in the matter of going on with it. And why should it not be?
Contrast public ownership, and the success that has been obtained in western Ontario, with private ownership of railways

in Canada and in some other countries of the world. I have never yet heard the statement contradicted that practically every privately owned railway in the United States has, at some time or another, been in the hands of a receiver. The Canadian Northern railway has been cited here as an example of the failure of private ownership, and no better example could be given. Three hundred million dollars from the public treasury went into that railway under private ownership. And yet it failed. We sometimes hear of the Canadian Pacific and of the success which it has attained. That is quite true, and I have absolutely no criticism to make of that system. It is a well managed railway and a benefit to the people of Canada; but the success of that company is not entirely the result of their own efficiency. Even to-day a very substantial proportion of their dividends is based on the benefits and grants of land which they received from the Dominion of Canada.
It is the fashion to-day to decry public ownership. So much so that I am sometimes tempted to think-and any remarks I may make in this direction are nor directed at any gentlemen who have spoken or may speak-I am tempted to believe that the fashion has been inaugurated as the result of definite propaganda on the part of private ownership interests as against public ownership.
By which organization?
I do not believe it would be very difficult for the imagination of hon. members in this House to tell just exactly what I am thinking about.
Do not impute motives.

I am not imputing any motive to anybody, and if those who are interested in private enterprises are now doing their best to discredit public ownership, I am not sure that I can find a great deal of fault with them, because, after all, self preservation is the first law of nature. But for the public in general consistently and persistently to close its eyes to the undoubted fact that private ownership has been a failure is rather more than I can understand. No one expects that the national railways are going to succeed unless certain changes are made. We must consolidate the roads. We must cut out unnecessary duplication and unnecessary overhead expenses. That is going to take time, and I, for one, would
express the opinion, off-hand, that it will take a period of at last four or five years to enable us to decide whether the great experiment which we are making will be a success or a failure. I presume it would be rank heresy for anyone to say in this House that the failure of the Grand Trunk was a blessing in disguise, because it would not have been possible, to make the national railway a success without the inclusion of the Grand Trunk Railway. I do not think that it was possible for the Canadian Northern, combined with the Grand Trunk Pacific, to make a success of operation unless they had in Ontario some such freight gathering agency as is supplied by the Grand Trunk. The Grand Trunk supplies in the east what the Canadian Northern did not have. The Canadian Northern supplies in the west what the Grand Trunk did not have, and a proper co-ordination and consolidation of the two carefully made ought to give us a system that will be able to compete, on something like even terms, with the Canadian Pacific Railway.
There is another point which has not been brought out. It seems to be the impression throughout Canada, in the press and in the House, that the whole purpose of public railway operation is the making of profit-financial profit. That is not the purpose of public ownership at all. The primary purpose of public ownership is to give service to the people and to give it at cost. I frankly admit that it would be bad business to operate the national railways with a view only to give service, having no regard at all as to whether the railways would carry themselves or not. But, primarily, the object of public ownership is to give service to the people, and the primary object of private ownership is to make profit, and service on a privately operated railway line is merely a secondary matter and a means to an end.
It is extremely regrettable that the test of public ownership, or public operation of railroads, comes at a most inauspicious time and under the most unfavourable circumstances. The Government was forced to take over these roads. They were taken over by a government that was not in sympathy with the principle of public ownership, although the Acting Prime Minister, Sir Thomas White, tried to make a virtue of necessity, and declared that his party was the party of public ownership. However, that claim was dropped very soon afterwards, and has not been repeated by any government since. A

parliament which did not believe in the principle was forced to take it over, and we were forced to make the test of public ownership under conditions which made financial success almost impossible for a good many years to come. Thus public ownership is charged by its foes with losses for which it is not logically responsible. Thus also an ideal situation was created for the opponents of the principle, and if they had had the selecting of the battle ground on which to fight their foes, they could not have chosen any better ground than the one upon which they stand to-day. Here was public ownership making headway day by day, in many parts of Canada. Municipalities were making a success of managing their public utilities in various parts of the country. Hydro had been a success. Labour was asking that the principle be applied much further than had ever been done before. It asked that it be applied to all the great public services upon which the convenience and the prosperity of the great mass of the people depend, such as telephones, telegraphs, control of water powers and other great natural resources. That feeling was making progress throughout Canada. Then providentially for the purpose of those who are opposed to public ownership, a situation was created which lent itself to the discrediting of the hated principle. What, then, was more easy, or natural, or misleading, than to frame the syllogism, with its false conclusions, that certain railways were losing money, that these railways were publicly owned and publicly controlled, and, therefore, that public ownership was responsible for the loss and would always result in failure. I say that public ownership up to this time in the national railway field has never had a fair chance. I want to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for his courage, during the election campaign when he made the statement that the national railways shall be given a fair trial, which statement has since translated into government policy. I also congratulate the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) because of his pronouncements in that regard. But a fair trial means good management free from politics and the consolidation of the railways at as early a moment as possible. It means also retaining the confidence of the people of Canada in the sincerity of the Government as to its declared railway policy. That is absolutely essential. I believe in the sincerity of the Government, 'Mr. Euler.]
but I say that it becomes the duty of the Government, and of its followers, if we are to give public ownership and operation of the railways a fair trial, to do nothing that may create distrust in the minds of the people. That is why I deprecate the criticism from this side of the House.
The national railways have one tremendous advantage over any private railway; it has been referred to very seldom, and I do not know that anyone has spoken of it in this debate. If the people themselves have confidence in the government and in the management of the road, they will take a pride in what is their own and patronize it. It will be the duty of the board which is to be appointed in due course to cultivate that feeling, and to educate the people to the desirability and the necessity of patronizing that which belongs to them. I would say that it makes a very strong combination when you impress upon the public that in supporting their own railways, they are also serving their own financial interests. I venture to suggest that even today privately owned railway systems are not quite so sure as they were that the National Railways are not going to be a success and are already feeling the competition which greater efficiency has brought. For example, we have an excellent passenger service between Toronto and Ottawa. It is only two or three years ago when, if a man desired to obtain a lower berth on the Canadian Pacific, he had to reserve it two or three days ahead, whereas he could always get a lower berth on the National Railways right up to the last moment. That condition of affairs is pretty well reversed, and it is because the National Railways are giving service. It is also because the people are beginning to think they ought to patronize that which belongs to them. In this, I reflect in no way upon the service given by the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is excellent.
I have not gone into figures nor into details, because I do not think it is necessary to do so. The question is largely one of principle. I, for one, believe that the people of Canada have, in themselves, the genius, patriotism and self-sacrifice, if necessary, to succeed in the great work to which they have put their hands. But it will be a very difficult fight, if this Parliament or its members are the cause of any doubt arising in the mind of the people as to our sincerity in our efforts to give public ownership a fair chance. Let those who believe in the principle say so in this House

and elsewhere and let those who cannot say so, await results, meanwhile doing nothing to prejudice the great experiment. I believe, if we do that honestly, the time will come -and it is not so very far distant-when Canadians will say that the nationalisation of these great roads was in the interest of the people of Canada.

I do not rise to oppose the estimate and, therefore, I shall not take up much of the time of this committee. It has been rather surprising that the discussion on this estimate has centred largely around the principle of government ownership. I am unable to see the relevancy of the discussion inasmuch as we have government ownership of railways now, and the estimate, I presume, is to continue their operation. I do not, of course, profess to be a man schooled in the strategy of politics; but I would hazard the opinion that hon. members on the government side who have spoken against public ownership, have been compromising their party, for, if government ownership is a failure, it will be said, no doubt, that it could not be anything else when run by a government that did not believe in public ownership. If it be a success, that will be proof that their judgment was bad. It might be well just to "wait a wee," as the Scotchman says, before you come to your conclusions. Hon. members opposite, however, do not need any advice from me along that line. It is, of course, reasonable to suppose that when a government is opposed to a principle, it will make a bad job of administration. That is not always true; as a matter of fact the Liberal party has traditionally been opposed to tariffs, and yet it has made an excellent job of administering tariffs. It has done it equally as well as the Conservative party has done. While a number of Government supporters may be opposed to the principle of public or government ownership, I have no doubt the Liberal party will make, perhaps, as good a job of administering government-owned railways as it will do in administering a tariff, and if it does that, we shall be perfectly satisfied with the result.
Government ownership of railways may not be the solution that we are looking for; but hon. gentlemen who have spoken against it ought to be fair and admit the fact that the taking over of the Canadian Northern was not merely because the government of the day believed in government ownership, but because of the necessity
brought about by a government subsidized line on the verge of bankruptcy and when hon. members of the present Government criticise the action of the former government in this regard, they have failed to tell us what should have been done under the circumstances. Would they have subsidized the railway further, or would they have sold it out for a song to a private company and given one railway company a monopoly of the railway business of the country? Or, what would they have done? I think we can safely leave that question aside and deal with the fact that we have at the present moment a government-owned railway, and that the job is to run it. It has been demonstrated that private ownership of that road was a failure. If it be heresy, as my hon. friend (Mr. Euler) remarked, to say that the failure of the Grand Trunk was a blessing in disguise, it could not be any more than heresy to hope for the failure of the Canadian Pacific also that we might have another and a larger blessing in disguise. That would help us to consolidate further and to have a real government-owned system of railways in Canada. I doubt very much whether we can hope for complete success of government-owned railways in this country while they are being run in competition with a large company that has been subsidized also from the public treasury. Therefore,. I hope that, some day, instead of speaking against government ownership of a part of our Canadian lines, hon. members of this House will be advocating government ownership of all the lines in Canada.
Never.

An hon. gentleman opposite says: "Never." It is very easy to say that, of course, but it does not get him anywhere. The same could have been said of a thousand things that are to-day in practice. I presume the same hon. gentleman would have said: We shall never be able to fly in the air; but we are doing so now, and what he is "nevering" about now will be in vogue soon.
I have a suggestion or two to make, and I think I can say before six o'clock what I want to say. If co-operation be necessary to the success of business, it is, perhaps, more necessary on government railways than anywhere else. I believe that it will contribute largely to the success of the enterprise if the highest possible degree of co-operation can be secured along the whole line of administering that business. I am glad to think that the Prime Minister

(Mr. Mackenzie King) has gone on record in his book on "Industry and Humanity" for the principle of co-operation in running large public utilities; that is, that there should be co-operation between the public, the owners and the workers engaged in the industry. I would like to suggest very briefly that the present Government, in the operation of the Canadian National Railways, should adhere to that principle and that the great masses of the people who are engaged in running the railways, should have their quota of representation on the railway board in order that the highest possible degree of co-operation may be secured in the enterprise.
Furthermore, I should like to point out to the Government-it is not, of course, necessary to do so, because they know it better than I do-that one of the largest items in the deficit on our government railways is for interest charges. I believe I am right in saying that. I think the interest for last year amounted to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $17,000,000. Allowing, on the capital expenditure of over $471,000,000, 3i per cent interest, we shall have approximately $17,000,000. Now, with a running tap of that nature it is not likely that we are going to be able to keep the reservoir full, and I urge that the Government take into consideration the possibility of turning the tap off. I have asked on previous occasions, and I ask again, is it possible for the Government to finance its own railways, financed for and by the Government in such a way as to eliminate interest? I would advise them to make the experiment along this line, and if it prove successful in this particular instance it may be possible to apply it to all other government operations and ultimately make it the national policy to finance every industry in Canada.
Now, it is six o'clock, and although I should like to say some other things I do not wish to detain the committee. I shall therefore sum up my remarks by saying that we need, first of all, co-operation in this great enterprise, among all the people working on it, as well as on the part of the representatives of the public and the Government, and I ask that the Government appoint a representative of labour, not only on the railway board of directors, but on the Board of Railway Commissioners. I would also emphasize the necessity of investigating the possibility of securing our own loans for the National Railways

from our own treasury and thereby save interest to the people of Canada.

Of course, there is this difference between publicly-owned and privately-owned railways: those which are privately-owned take into consideration not only the question of service, but also the question of revenue with a view to paying dividends. It may be a long time before the Canadian National Railways pay a dividend, if they ever do; but if the quality of service which they render to the Canadian people is satisfactory, then the question of dividends is not a matter for consideration. It is not the hope that the nationally-owned railways will pay dividends; if they can come out even in the years to come, rates will be satisfactorily reduced until the cost of upkeep and general maintenance is at a minimum.
Not only must we have co-ordination of the systems included in our National Railways, but we must place them on a sound business basis. The railways should be taken altogether out of politics. That is one reason why I favour public ownership: because corrupt influences are often exerted in governmental circles as the result of private ownership. When we acquire a railway on behalf of the people; when it belongs to the people and they take an interest in it, it should be removed from the influence of politics and placed on a sound business basis; that is the only way, I believe, in which a nationally owned railway can be made to pay.
But there is more than that. I think the speech of the minister was good all the way through; it was optimistic, and there was a policy involved. But there is one point in the policy which I think is faulty, and that is the lack of any intention to continue to build branch lines. It is a well known fact that if the transcontinental railways that belong to Canada are ever to be made to pay, it will only be in respect of the traffic and business originating and carried on in that part of the system west of the Great Lakes, or west of Winnipeg. The trunk lines are already in existence and we know that alongside of these trunk lines the settlers are, and have been for many years. All the products of the farm are going to those lines and the only way we can bring prosperity to the national lines, is, in a measure, to increase the service. But how are we going to increase the service if we cut off all feeders to the trunk lines? There are various ways in which this matter can be dealt with. One way in which we can increase the service of the transcontinental railways is by increasing the number of people on each side of them. Looking over the statistics of immigration during the last twenty years, I find that 3,428,834 people have come into Canada, but of these, 2,000,000 have remained on this side of the Great Lakes, and only 1,423,538 have settled in the three prairie provinces.
I understand that contiguous to these lines to-day there are over thirty million acres of land not settled, and for that reason we must direct the stream of immigration to the West, so that these people will settle on the farms and increase the productivity of the land, thereby providing more business for the railways. It is only by increased service that we can get an increased revenue for the railways and place them on a paying basis.

I am not interested in that question at the moment. What I am interested in is this. Last year the Minister of Railways promised the people in my district that a certain railway extension would be completed. He said to these people: If you will go into that village and build an elevator we will see to it that the line is completed. In order that there may be no doubt whatver I will read what the minister said:
Hon. Mr. Reid: In speaking to Mr. Hanna about the maitter he mentioned that they would lay this ten miles this year for the reason that an elevator would be built, and it was for that purpose the rails would be laid. I am quite satisfied that it is the intention of the Canadian National Railway management to lay the ten miles in quesion, and I feel satisfied from the way Mr Hanna mentioned it to me that there is no doubt it will be done. Unless something unforeseen should happen it is the intention anyway to lay the rails before that time. The 50,000 tons of new rails which were purchased are now being rolled and sent on to the main line. On this promise of the minister the people went into that village-the construction way had already been laid, but not the rails-and the village came into existence and an elevator was built, people put more crops into the ground, and then last year, when the crop was harvested, they had no railway to take it out. At the present time these people are anxiously awaiting the fulfilment of this promise, which was made not only on one occasion, but repeatedly since 1918. It seems to me that if the national railways are ever going to pay, you must build these branch lines in order to serve as feeders to the trunk lines. It is poor economy, in my view, to cut off the branch lines. You cannot do that and reasonably expect the trunk lines to pay.
In looking over this item of $42,000,000 which is to be expended on this road, I find that only a very small amount is to be devoted to construction, namely, $1,286,164. This to me seems a very small amount, and I do believe that it would be in the interests of this great system to send out small feeders into the country to encourage the farmers-the wheat growers and the
[ Mr. Lewis. ]
dairymen-to put more seed into the land and intensify their farming, and thus provide a greater volume of business for the railways that are on our hands at the present time. That would be real economy, and it would result in a larger share of business for the national railways, and in the sum total be the means of making them
pay-
I trust that in the near future when these roads are co-ordinated, the men in charge will look into this aspect of the question and see to it that small branch lines, not very extensive ones, but lines that will reach to the people and bring business to the main line are built. Such a policy will produce a revenue that will probably put the railways on a paying basis.

The speeches that have been delivered to-day have been very interesting, perhaps instructive, but very largely academic. The speakers appear to have overlooked some facts which, if recognized, might perhaps have made the speeches shorter.
The first fact is that the country finds itself to-day the owner and possessor of about 22,000 miles of railway. The second fact is that the Government finds itself obliged to take over these railways. The third fact is that the Government has announced its policy to own and operate these railways, and to give that policy a fair trial. The fourth fact, I think, is that a large majority of the members of this House are prepared to support the policy of the Government. I think that the members of this House have sufficient information at the present time to enable them to give an intelligent vote on this question. I further think that a majority of the people of this country are prepared to support the Government's policy, and that those of them who take an interest in the question are fairly well informed. Therefore, I think that further speeches would not give much information, and I would respectfully suggest that under these circumstances we cut out any more speeches, proceed to business, pass the estimate, and advance towards the end of the session

I shall try as far as possible to follow the advice, with which I do not quarrel' very much, of the hon. member for King's, but there are just one or two matters to which I desire to make reference.

Supply-Railivays
In the first place, I agree with the last speaker that a number at least of the addresses to which we have listened this afternoon have been academic discussions of the question of public versus private ownership. I do not propose to follow the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rin-fret), the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean), or the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) through their discussion for and against public ownership and government operation of railways. I do desire to say this, however, that it is gratifying to the party who sit in this end of the House, and who represent what is here to-day of the late government, to find that all parties in the House to-day are endorsing the policy of railway management which was inaugurated by the government which was in power up to the 6th of December last. Both from those who favour government ownership and operation, and those who are opposed to that policy and favour private ownership, and who sit uipon the government side of the House, we have the assurance that it is their wish that government ownership as at present carried on by the present Government, and by its predecessor, shall be given a fair trial.
It does seem to me, however, that it would be consistent, at least, for some of these gentlemen to explain to the House when they became convinced that the present system was the best system in the interests of Canada at the present time. It is a fact that up to the 6th of last December, when all the information that we now have was available to men in public life, there was no feature in connection with the policy of the late government which was more severely and intensely denounced and repudiated by its opponents than its railway policy. However, I am not going to attempt to follow hon. gentlemen opposite through their various stages to their present position on that question. Nevertheless, it does seem to me that it would be desirable for the member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) to confer with the member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell) and the member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), and possibly with the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), and that these gentlemen should try and reconcile their positions upon this great question.
I want to say this: That so far as the policy of the late government-which is the policy of the present Government in connection with the management of the
National Railways-goes,	that policy
was arrived at without any question of public or private ownership; it was arrived at by reason of the fact that the late government was forced to provide for the management of these railways which were practically left on its door-step. I do not think that it matters very much who was to blame for that. The question as to whether the Liberal party or the old Liberal-Conservative party was responsible for Canada's railway problem has been a fruitful matter for political discussion for many years. It has been threshed out in past parliaments and in past elections, until it is possibly a threadbare matter for political discussion today. The fact is, Mr. Chairman, that the late government was forced to solve the question of handling the railways which became national property during the war; and I do not think there is any real opinion in Canada to-day that will question the wisdom of that policy at the time it was arrived at by the late government. In that connection let me refer for a moment to what the member for St. James said with reference to the subsidies which have been paid out to the old Canadian Northern system. He divided the periods during which subsidies were given into the period prior to 1911, and the period since and showed, of necessity, that a very large proportion of the amount which had been paid in subsidies and in cash advances to the Canadian Northern was paid over to them subsequently to 1911. No one will dispute that, but why were these subsidies paid? The reason is very clearly set out in the address of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier on May 13, 1914 when, in discussing the Canadian Northern loan, which was then before the House, he made this statement:
In 1899, or thereabouts, alter we came into office we asked Parfliament to give them assistance to extend the railway system then in exiistence in Manitoba eastward to the end of Lake Superior. If I remember rightly we gave them a cash subsidy of $6,400 a mile for that length of railway. Later in 1903 we induced parliament to give them a guarantee of $13,000 a mile for a line of railway running through Manitoba to the city of Edmonton. Afterwards, in 1908, we asked Parliament to give them another guarantee of bonds to provide for several branch lines which would be feeders of the line in the prairie provinces. In 1911, as has been explained by my right hon. friend, it was considered that the system would not be complete unless it were extended eastward to tthe St. Lawrence and eventually to the maritime provinces, that is to say unless it was made a transcontinental railway, and in that year we asked Parliament to give to the enter-
Supply-Railways

prise from Port Arthur to Montreal a guarantee of bonds to the extent of $25,000 a mile. After the new government came into office they took up the policy which we inaugurated. In 1912 Parliament was asked to assist a line from St. Albert to the limits of the province of British Columbia, a distance of 115 miles, witih a subsidy of $35,000 a mile.
My hon. friend from St. James is entirely correct when he states that large sums were paid in subsidies to the Canadian Northern system subsequent to 1911, but these subsidies were paid in pursuance of obligations and commitments made by the government prior to 1911. I am not quarrelling with the wisdom of that policy, but what I object to is that an attempt should be made to show that these payments were made as a result of the action of the government which came into power in 1911.
What was the policy of the late government with reference to the management of the Canadian National Railways, and after all that is the question that goes to the very root of the matter? When the late government was forced to provide a system for the control and management of the railways which became its property a system was adopted which has recommended itself to the present Government, and which meets with the approval of hon. gentlemen to the left, and it was this: To provide for the control of these railways, for the management of the system, by an independent board freed entirely from political control, and I agree with hon. gentlemen opposite that it is only by carrying out that policy that there can be any future for the National system. The management must be free from political control.
In the report which the Minister of Railways presented to the House on April 11, for the calendar year 1921, there was a very full statement given of the operations of the National lines, and I would like to draw attention to this fact: That report covered the railway operations for a period during the whole of which, with the exception of two days, the late government was in power, and it is a matter of satisfaction to those who were associated with the late administration to know that in the report there was not one word of criticism of anything that the previous government had done in connection with railway operation. The very greatest compliment that could be paid to the late government in connection with the operation of these railways is to be found in the fact that no report ever presented to this House dealing with the work of any public department has met with

more general approval than the report brought down on April 11. There has not been one word of criticism of that report in this House; nothing but the warmest words of commendation have been heard. Similar commendation has appeared in the press of the country irrespective of political alignment, and I say that speaks as strongly as anything possibly could for the policy of the late government. Furthermore the policy adopted by the late government for the management of the National Railways providing for a unified board was crystallized into law and is on the statute books of Canada to-day, and that policy we are assured by the present Minister of Railways will be carried out.
I am not going to further discuss the general railway policy but I do want to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for St. Antoine yesterday.
I have no desire to introduce again the discussion with reference to the advance purchases of supplies made under the provisions of the Order in Council of 6th October, 1921, but I want to say that my hon. friend from St. Antoine has confused the issue, I think, in the minds of the public, and I think he is possibly confused himself, ii I read his statements in Hansard aright as to the part the government played with reference to the ordering of supplies. I refer to it again for this reason: that the point raised by the hon. member from St. Antoine strikes at the very root of the whole system of government operation or control of the National system. If political considerations are to influence the board of management of the National system, then I agree with my hon. friend from St. Antoine that it would be a most dangerous thing for the future of the system. I know of nothing more dangerous than that the board in control of our National Railways should in any way be influenced by political considerations in their administration. If we reach the time when they are influenced and affected by political considerations we will have struck a blow from which it would be impossible to recover.
Reference has been made so often to the Order in Council of the 6th October, and the Order in Council of the 13th August that, it seems to me, these documents should be read into the record, in order that it may be complete, and I propose to place in the record, first the Order in Council of the 13th August, 1921, which is known as Order No. 2861, and reads as follows:
The Committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 9th August.
