1921, from the Minister of Railways and Canals, representing that, by an Order in Council of the 21st of April, 1921, (PC. 1403) authority was given for the ordering by the management of the Canadian National Railways from the Algoma Steel Corporation, of 50,000 gross tons of 85-pound steel rails at $55 a ton, f.o.b. Sault Ste. Marie, Ont., and from the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, of 20,000 gross tons of 85-pound steel rails, f.o.b. Sydney, N.S., at the same price.
Of the 50,000 tons ordered from the Algoma Steel Corporation, approximately 39,000 tons have been delivered to date, leaving a balance of 11,000 tons which may not be required this year. The Algoma Steel Corporation suggest that this balance be rolled and put in stock, to be shipped out when required, any tonnage accepted before the end of the present year to be paid for at the above mentioned price, and the tonnage held over to be delivered at the price which' may be agreed upon for rails for early spring delivery next year. In connection with this suggestion, and also with reference to the requirements for next year, Mr. D. B. Hanna, president of the Canadian National Railways, advises, as follows:
"The present probabilities are that we will not require more rails this year, but it would be quite in order, as a matter of convenience to the Steel Corporation, to roll the balance (approximately eleven thousand tons) at their convenience, subject to a price to be fixed for next year's requirements, such price not to exceed the price quoted to other Canadian railways.
"The outlook for employment next winter is not satisfactory at present, and I would suggest for your consideration the passing of an Order in Council, authorizing us to place a contract at an early date for forty thousand tons of rails (which is in addition to the eleven thousand tons referred to) for winter rolling, as we will require the tonnage, and if we can indicate to Mr. Franz that the rails will be required, it will enable him to take in sufficient raw materials in the shape of coal and iron ore before navigation closes, and thus permit him to give us a substantially lower price per ton than present year's prices."
The Minister, on the advice of the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, recommends that authority be given for carrying out the suggestions of Mr. Hanna with reference to the said balance of 11,000 tons of rails remaining undelivered this year, and to the quantity of 40,000 tons required next year; the price to be paid for the 40,000 tons to be agreed upon, but not to exceed lowest prices paid by other Canadian railways, and payments to be made as deliveries taken.
The committee advise that the requisite authority be granted accordingly.
That is the Order in Council passed on the 13th day of August, 1921, and it agrees as to date with the statement of the hon. member from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) as to unemployment, made in the early stage of this debate. On the 13th August, before there was any question of an election, or any statement or thought as to the dissolution of the House, the question of unemployment was raised in the communication of the President of the Canadian National Board to the Minister of Railways as set out in the Order in Council itself.
In order that we may follow as to date, let me read to the House, next, a letter, dated 13th September, 1921, from the President of the Canadian National Board to the Minister of Railways of that date. The letter is dated Toronto, September 13th, 1921, and reads:
Toronto, Ont., September, 1921.
My dear Doctor,-
Referring to conversation regarding repairs to Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian National freight cars.
In the early months of the year indications pointed to a substantial recession in freight traffic, and to meet this condition we made a substantial reduction in our forces over the entire System and at all important divisional points in the hours of labour of such men we carried on the pay rolls. The effect of this in our repair work was very noticeable. We sidetracked a very large number of freight cars, until at the present time we have approximately 8,0-00 cars waiting repairs. Of this number, either in partial service or side-tracked on repair tracks, there are not less than 2,0-00 Grand Trunk Pacific cars. Many of these cars have been out of service for a period of time before we had anything to do with the management of that Company, and having regard to the fact that most of the Grand Trunk Pacific equipment has been in service around fifteen years, it follows that a large number have yet to be repaired, or rather rebuilt. This leaves approximately 6,000 National System cars in bad order. It is estimated that 3,000 of these require more or less heavy repairs, and the work to be done on the balance of 3,000 is of a minor nature or what is called running repairs, and will be restored to service by our own shopmen.
It occurs to me, in view of wide spread unemployment, that the car plants of the different operating companies are* in respect of some of them at all events, closed down; that in all probability the Dominion Government will be called upon this fall and winter to help out the situation with cash contributions to an unemployment fund, it might be a good move to distribute to these plants sufficient cars requiring heavy repairs (having regard to their daily output) to keep the companies going during the winter and into the early spring months, with the hope that conditions will have improved by that time to take up much of the unemployed forces.
The following plants, I am advised, are and have been closed down for some months:-
Fort William plant,
Eastern Car Company's plant, New Glasgow,
Amherst plant,
and the following plants partly under operation :
National plant, Hamilton,
Canadian Car and Foundry plant, Montreal.
The need for repairing all of our equipment, including the Grand Trunk Pacific equipment, from a traffic standpoint, is not a vital one, as we are with our own organization able to keep up our ordinary running repairs. But it does seem to me, if the unemployment situation can be to some extent relieved as suggested in this letter, we should be authorized to

Supply-Railways
make arrangements to put as much of our equipment as possible into good repair, even though, because of trade conditions, many of ihese cars are, after being repaired, side-tracked waiting for loads. In other words, instead of handing out contributions to an unemployment fund, It would be much better to use the funds proposed to be expended in that connection and authorize us to negotiate with the car plants to do repair work for the National System.
Please let me hear from you.
Whom is that letter from?

As I stated when I read it, it is a letter addressed by the President of the Canadian National board, Mr. Hanna, to the Minister of Railways at that date.
Nothing further, so far as my knowledge goes, occurred until the 6th of October, 1921, when the following Order in Council was passed:

The Committee of the Privy Council have had before them a report, dated 4th October, 1921, from the Minister of Railways and Canals, stating that, in his capacity as Minister of Railways, he has discussed with the Canadian National management, and with the chief executives of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, the question of unemployment in its relation to the railways now under Government control and operation.
*Serious consideration has been given to the possibility of the National railways (including the Grand Trunk) so anticipating their requirements as to permit the placing in the immediate future of next year's orders for rails and accessories, and for the rebuilding and repair of freight equipment, in order that present unemployment may be relieved, and work provided during the winter months.
Under normal conditions, it is the practice to pflace such orders during the early spring months, and to confine rebuilding and repair work, as far as possible, to system shops. The minister believes that, in view of the present abnormal industrial situation, the usual practice might well be varied to the extent of placing, at an early date, next year's orders for rails and accessories, and, in addition to repair work now being done in railway shops, by arranging with the various equipment companies though-ou't Canada to participate in the rebuilding and repair of freight equipment.
In doing so, however, it is only fair to the railways, that expenditures so incurred shall not be considered a charge against the current year's operation or financing, and while the management will make every effort to see that repair work undertaken outside the railway shops is done at fair and reasonable prices, any increased expenditure involved should not be a charge against the railways, but against such financial provision as may from time to time be made by the Government to deal with unemployment.
And in order that there may be no question of considerations other than unemployment influencing the placing of these orders, the minister suggests that the allocation of this business be on the concurrence of the Minister of Uabour, whose departmental officials are closely in touch with conditions affecting labour

throughout Canada, and whose officials shall co-operate with the officials of the Department of Railways in dealing with this situation so far a it affects the railways under Government control.
In order that the management may have a free hand and that the business may be distributed 'to best advantage, it is considered advisable that the Order in Council to authorize the purchase of 40,000 tons of rails from the Algoma 'Steel Corporation for next year's delivery be cancelled, and that such new business as may be given the Algoma Steel Corporation be contingent upon the general situation as it may develop.
The minister, therefore, recommends, on the advice of the deputy Minister of Railways and Canals, that Order in Council of the 13th August, 1921 (P. C. 2861) granting authority to the management to order 40,000 tons of 85 lb. steel rails from the Algoma Steel Corporation for next year's delivery be and hereby is cancelled in so far as it relates to the 40,000 tons in question.
That, having due regard to the unemployment situation, as well as the requirements of the railways, the management of Canadian National Railways and the management of the Grand Trunk railway be authorized to order on next year's account, and not exceeding next year's prices, a maximum of 75,000 tons of rails and necessary accessories, and to arrange for the rebuilding or repair of 2,000 cars at suitable points at fair and reasonable charges, and that the expenditure so incurred be provided for in the Supplementary Estimate to be brought down at the next ensuing session of Parliament.
That in placing orders for the rebuilding and repair of freight equipment, the charges against the railways shall only be the falir and reasonable cost of the same in the company's shops, and that any extra expense involved be a proper charge against unemployment generally and regarded as such.
That in neither case shall expenditures incurred this year in anticipation of next year's requirements be chargeable against current operation or finance.
The Committee concur in the foregoing recommendation and submit the same for approval.
(Sgd) Rodolphe Boudreau,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
In pursuance of this last Order in Council, the cars referred to by the President of the Canadian National Board in his letter of the 13th of September were placed as follows: 500 cars were contracted for with the National plant at Hamilton; 500 with the Canada Car and Foundry plant at Montreal; 500 went to Amherst and 500 to New Glasgow. For the Grand Trunk Pacific, there were 1,000 cars that went to Fort William, and that order was placed and authorized in pursuance of the order appointing the receiver; it was approved by the Exchequer Court of Canada.
The point I desire to make in connection with this, is that the Orders in Council were absolutely necessary in order to enable the board to contract for car repairs, and

to purchase the rails. The board had no authority under the law to proceed, without the authority of the government through an Order in Council. The reason for that is this: Last session Parliament in its estimates provided certain sums for these purposes. As regards the expenditure of the sum authorised in the estimate of last year, the amount could be expended by the board upon the authority of the estimates; but when the question became one of anticipating the requirements of the road and ordering, in the fiscal year 1921-22, rails and car repairs that would naturally fall into the fiscal year 1922-23, it became necessary, for the purpose of financing and preventing the amount being a charge against the fiscal year 1921-22, that an Order in Council should be passed. The point which I desire to make clear if I can is, that as regards any of the items authorised in the Order in Council of the 6th of October, not one dollar's worth went into the operations of the fiscal year 192122, as would appear to have been the idea of the hon. member for St. Antoine. Not one dollar of that would operate to improve the financial statement for the past year.
If we admit unemployment and if we admit the wisdom of the late government in anticipating, during the past winter months, the requirements which would be inevitable when we reached April, May and the summer months, then surely no question can be raised as to the wisdom of the late government's policy. If we admit that unemployment existed, if we admit that there was any duty or obligation upon the government to relieve that unemployment, so far as it lay in the power of the government to relieve it, the logic of the late government's position is irresistible.
I wish to refer to one other matter, the point raised as to the great improvement that took place during the four months of August, September, October and November, 1921, an operating account. I do not think any one ever claimed that the late government was entitled to credit for that. If the claim has been made I have never heard it. The point was answered by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) last night. It is to be explained by the fact that during these months we reached the peak in grain transportation, and consequently it was a natural result that we should have had an improvement in operation account.	.

Yesterday when I referred to this matter I pointed out that
the whole saving of $20,000,000 was in operating expense account, so that the question of increased freight during those months would not affect the statement I submitted to the House.

I was referring to the point as it arose in the address of my hon. friend from Marquette. He referred particularly to the increase in freight, and I thought that my hon. friend (Mr. Mitchell) had done the same. But a review of the financial operations of the Canadian Pacific Railway during the same four months will reveal that in that period they also showed a substantial increase on operating account. While possibly the late government are not entitled to any credit for the results obtained during those four months, I am sure that my hon. friends opposite must rejoice that the greatly increased proportion of grain that was handled in 1921 played a large part in reducing the operating deficit for the year. I have nothing further to say in connection with this item, and I see no objection to its adoption.

I can say all that I wish to say in less than five minutes, because my views have been very fully expressed by the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and the member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). But there are two points which I should like to mention. I was very much surprised yesterday to hear the member for St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell) declare that he did not believe in the principle of public ownership of public utilities, and I took it that he based his belief upon his experience in the province of Quebec. If I am wrong in that interpretation of his remarks I stand to be corrected; but I would submit that the logic of the inference is decidedly questionable. Granting a break-down in public 'ownership, there are two causes: either the one assigned by the hon. member, or another one which he did not mention, and that is the lack of public spirit and the disposition on the part of those concerned to regard the public service as a happy hunting-ground for private graft. Of course, public ownership of public utilities will fail and must fail if that is the attitude of the individuals who have to do with them. And there is a very different interpretation which may be put upon the facts as submitted yesterday in that connection, an interpretation which, I think, the hon. member would hardly care to impute to his native province. But public ownership of public utilities need

not fail. It has not failed in thousands of cases, and it will not fail, given a reasonable amount of honesty and public spirit. We are not asking for the application of public ownership to our farms and thousands of other businesses. But in connection with natural monopolies, whether they be municipal, provincial or federal, the conditions, I submit, are such as to render public ownership the wise, the prudent and the right policy.
Now, there has no doubt been a great deal of bungling in the past in regard to our railways, and things have reached a pass which is very regrettable. We have to face the conditions, and I just want in conclusion to deal with one suggestion that has been pressed in this House during the past two days as a solution of these difficulties, and that is, the getting rid of our National Railways. Well, who is going to buy them? There is only one concern in Canada that can take the National Railways off our hands, and that is the Canadian Pacific Railway. And if they did, what would be the result? You would have a practical monopoly of all railway transportation in Canada. In that connection I might refer to an article I read in the Grain Growers' Guide a few years ago in which it was stated that 42 men whose names were given, all but three of them residing in the cities of Montreal and Toronto, through interlocking directorates, had what might be described as a strangle hold on nearly all the manufacturing, transportation and financial interests of this country. Now, if the Canadian Pacific Railway were to absorb our National Railway system, and the Bank of Montreal should continue the absorption of our banks, what a huge octopus we should then have controlling the whole transportation and financial machinery of this country. I say, without casting any aspersions on the gentlemen concerned, that such a condition as that is a menace to democracy in this country, even though the parties who constitute such an enormous corporation might be angels. I wish to declare, and lay down as a principle, altogether apart from the character of the people involved, that this is a state of things which we ought not to permit in this country. And it is a condition of affairs that is apparently in anticipation in certain quarters. That is all I have to say in this connection. I wish to endorse the points of view presented by the member for Marquette and the member for North Waterloo.

I merely wish to make a short comment and to ask a question or two. This Government has been in power for four and a half months. On the 8th March we were told in the Speech from the Throne that it was the policy of the Government to co-ordinate the railways, thereby effecting economies; and it was stated that that would be done at an early date. Later, on the 11th of April, this declaration was emphasized in
9 p.m. the very excellent remarks which were made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy). I have been informed upon what I consider reliable authority that the consolidation of the government owned roads would save to this country at least $50,000 a day. My information is that the estimate is even larger. Now, while I am always anxious to be on the safe side, yet if I had the choice of $50,000 a day on one hand, and, on the other, the unknown figure, I would choose the latter, because I am certain that the consolidation of the railways would effect a greater saving than $50,000 a day. That amount in less than twenty days would equal all that was paid during the last fiscal year by way of duty on agricultural implements coming into Canada. In less than twenty days-to make the matter personal-it would pay the indemnities of all the members of this House. In fourteen days it would pay the amount that the Minister of Militia (Mr. Graham) struck off his estimates and which we wish was still there. There is no doubt that every succeeding sun finds a loss settled upon this country, a loss that cannot be recovered. Nor can we make up at the other end what we are losing now; it is absolutely dead loss.
Now, I think if this were a business proposition it would be tackled iby a board of directors-business men-and some solution would long ago have been arrived at. By the way, I was told-and if it were not for this evidence to the contrary, I would be inclined to believe it-that the Minister of Railways was a strong, silent, business man. If he is not, there ought to be other men in the Cabinet who would take this matter into consideration and decide upon it. I am not one who believes that no one can be got in Canada to take up this important problem and settle it in a business way. I am satisfied that if it were committed to Mr. D. B. Hanna or to Mr. Mitchell, they could help us very much. At all events, there are business men in this country who, if they had to deal with this proposition,

would take it in hand at once; they would not permit loss to succeed loss as the days go on. Why, some hon. members of the House have been able to tell the minister how they would effect pronounced economies if they were asked to take the matter in hand. Surely something will be done long before the House prorogues to bring about what is so much desired by everybody. I would ask the minister then, if he ban say that my estimate of the saving which would be effected by the consolidation which he has promised is incorrect. If not correct, can he give me the estimate that he has? Finally, and most important, when is this thing going to be done in a business way?
Mr. KENNEDY Essex: I am not in a position to verify the statement that my hon friend (Mr. Ryckman) has given the committee as to what might be saved in the event of immediate consolidation, nor am I in a position to give, .to a dollar, the saving that would thus be brought about. But I may say that having in view the annual expenditure involved-. which, as the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) said yesterday, amounts to over 8330,000,000-perhaps we are justified in going slowly and carefully, in taking our time to see that the men who are placed in charge of this undertaking are men who will carry it to a successful conclusion. I may say that an example was set in this regard by the government which my hon. friend supported in the last election. They appointed their directors in May, 1921, and in their wisdom they decided to go slowly in the matter of consolidation. I think, perhaps, they were right. So far as the Government is concerned, we are going to bring about coordination as quickly as we can.

I have listened with some interest to the discussion of this important question. I look upon it as the greatest problem that faces the Government and the people to-day. Our attention is forcibly directed to the deficit we have to face. In order to enable the railways to pay their way, we have repeatedly raised the freight rates-to such an extent, in fact, that it is like the tariff for revenue; the higher the tariff, the less revenue we get. It is evident that the present rates do not permit the commerce of the country to move freely. I do not think there is any need of engaging experts, either from the United States or from Europe, as has been sug-
124i
gested, to tell us how we shall run our roads. But to the casual observer there seem to be several ways in which improvements could be made.
I believe there are many leaks at present, and these are apparent even to those who are not very well acquainted with railway matters. I will mention one or two. One is the expensive duplication of service over the lines in western Canada, and, I think, as well in eastern Canada. For instance, we have two lines west of Saskatoon running so close together for one hundred miles that you could hand a message from one train to the other. As if that incongruity were not complete in itself, express trains on both lines-on the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific,-run the same way at exactly the same time each day; service to the public is not considered at all. That has been going on for several months, and if attention is called to the matter we are told that a change cannot be made.
We have to evolve some method that will give the railway employees the proper viewpoint; that will bring them to realize that they are part owners, with the rest of the people of this country, of our national system. This may apply to the operators, engineers-yes, all the way down, even to the switchmen and sectionmen. Something should be done to give them the idea that the railways belong to them as well as to the rest of the people. It would be interesting to know what loss occurs annually in transit, due to breakages; for I believe that that loss could largely be prevented. I have no doubt the minister will give us that information before the discussion closes. In fact, I have even thought, Sir, that it may become necessary in some way to bonus the railway employees according to the length and quality of their service. Something will have to be done to offset this great waste.
It would be very interesting to know what the travelling expenses of certain officials over these lines are, their purpose in travelling, and whether such travel is really necessary. The hon. member for St. Antoine has said he did not believe in government ownership. Therefore, I take it he is not an unprejudiced observer of the government operation of railways. The fact remains that there is quite a suspicion in these days that those who have had the directing of these railways have not approached their task with a single eye to the successful operation
Supply-Railways

of a government owned and operated system. We must realize that we have these railways on our hands, and although perhaps we do not want them under our ownership all at once, there is nothing for it now but for the Government to make the best of it. At this time we need at the head of the railways men who believe in the system they are trying to run, who believe in government ownership, and have faith in their own ability.
We are always being reminded that the Canadian Pacific is a tremendous success, both as to service and profits. I myself am not so sure of that, in view of what it has cost the Canadian people to establish that great system. I think it is worth while to ask, when considering this question, what we have paid for the Canadian Pacific Railway. No great corporation was formed and built this system for the benefit of the people particularly, but this country has given to that company in money grants, cash subsidies, finished railways and lands, amounting, if we take a fair average valuation of the land, to a gift at the expense of the people of this country of nearly $40,000 for every mile the Canadian Pacific owns and operates to^ day. These figures were staggering to me when I first worked them out. Furthermore, the Canadian Pacific have always been the first to set the cost of service, and they have set it high enough to cover the cost of paying a dividend of 10 per cent yearly, and do some melon-cutting among themselves. In fact, I think some people have come to think that this country was developed for the sake of the Canadian Pacific Railway. But at last even this great company, I think, has come to realize that we have in the National Railways a system that is able to compete with them, and I am glad the minister has given it out as his policy that everything is to be done to give government ownership and operation a chance to succeed.
As far as the West is concerned, I know that the people there are proud of their national system, and that they will cooperate with the minister and with the directors of the road with a view to making this great system a success. But one thing they do ask of the minister and of the management, and that is that to the responsible positions in the system only men who believe in government ownership be appointed.
I think another factor that would help towards making the National Railways pay is a system of feeders. There are

many parts of the West to-day without railways, where settlers who went in many years ago expecting a railway are still without transportation facilities. In the prairie provinces some of these roads were projected and even surveyed while they were still under the control of the provincial governments, but these charters have been allowed to lapse. The Canadian Pacific have surveyed lines and obtained charters in certain parts of the country with the idea, I believe, of heading off the Canadian National system, and the settlers there are still without transportation facilities to market their produce. These charters were allowed to lapse and to-day the Canadian Pacific is seeking for the second time that I know of, to renew them. I hope the management of the Canadian National Railways will see to it that duplication, as far as possible, is eliminated, and that feeders will be built in those districts where they are so much needed at the present time.

What does the Government propose to do with regard to the bridge over the Red Deer river from Hanna to Medicine Hat? Is that going to be gone on with this year?
I have not the information here, but I shall be glad to get it and give it to my hon. friend at the next meeting of the committee.

I should like to go a little further into this matter. In western Canada at the present time, the Canadian National Railway have built many miles of roadbed on which at present there are no rails. Some of these roadbeds have been built over two years, and they were built for the purpose of giving the settlers in these various districts the accommodation they required. I understand from the minister that it is not the intention of the Government, or, so far as I know, of the railway officials, to lay rails on these roadbeds during this summer. I would point out to the House that at the

Supply-Railways
present time the people who live in these remote districts require transportation facilities. The roadbeds have been built in many places, and all that remains is for the steel to be laid. I think that the policy of keeping these people without transportation facilities, merely for the sake of not spending the money for laying the rails, is a policy that cannot be upheld under any circumstances whatever, and I would submit that the officials who are to be appointed to look after the National Railways should take into consideration this very important question at an early date. These roadbeds are deteriorating all the time, and they might just as well be made use of in order to serve the people in those remote districts. Some two or three days ago I received a letter from a man in the constituency I represent who resides alongside a piece of this completed roadbed on which no steel is laid-it is the Hanna-Medicine Hat branch of the Canadian Northern-and he tells me that no matter what the crop conditions are, there are over two hundred Hollander families who intend to pull out of that district unless the steel is laid there this year. They live right alongside the roadbed, and any one who knows the Hollanders as settlers in western Canada knows that they are perhaps the very best settlers we have. They are industrious and mind their own business. They are good farmers and they make very successful settlers. As I stated in this House two or three evenings ago, we have been spending millions of money to get people into this country and yet here are completed roadbeds of railways without steel on them, although by simply putting the steel on these roads we could attract the needed settlers. I maintain that the matter should be looked into and if possible steel should be laid wherever needed without further delay.

I want to ask the Minister of Railways a question. I am not going to speak on this matter, although I would very much like to do so, because in my constituency there is a short railway very similar to the one just spoken of. In this case also the ties are down, the road bed is built, and the people there are very anxious to have the railway completed and operated at once. If the line cannot be completed in any other way the farmers there would like to undertake the work themselves. Now, as to the question I desire to ask. Men who have travelled round the country considerably, and have
had an opportunity of knowing the conditions, tell me they have noticed very careless handling of freight at the freight sheds. During the Easter holidays, to mention a specific case, a man who is a cheese inspector said he was standing at a freight shed and noticed the railway employees turning over a box. He knew what was in the box and the value of its contents, and that it would break if not handled carefully. In a few minutes the box did break and the goods to the value of $12 were utterly destroyed. Folks have told me that they have noticed a great deal of this careless handling and I was just wondering whether the minister could give us any information on the subject. I shall not criticize the department, previous ministers, or anyone else because I realize how difficult it must be to keep tab on men when they are beyond the reach of a foreman, and it is difficult enough when the foreman is standing right over them; but I thought that possibly the minister might have some figures which would give an idea of the extent of the annual loss from this cause. I know the present minister has not been long in office and perhaps it might be difficult for him to give exact details, but even an approximate estimate would serve the purpose.

I feel indebted to the hon. member for bringing this matter to the attention of the committee, a matter which we are all interested in. I have had no report from the railway management in connection with it, or on the subject of breakages particularly, beyond the fact that they state that the breakages on the National Railways are not any more than they are on other lines. Just how much that represents I could not say, but I will bring the statement the hon. gentleman has made to the attention of the management, and I feel perfectly sure they will only be too glad to rectify such conditions if they exist.
Hon. JOHN B. M. BAXTER (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert) :	I doubt the wisdom of offering
any observations owing to the length of time the debate has already lasted and yet, Sir, feeling that in a good many matters that have been discussed I personally differ, in some respects, from what I might call the prevailing opinion I think there is perhaps an obligation on members to express their views. There has not been since this House opened, I think, a better or a more useful debate than the one which
Supply-Railways

is drawing near a close. It has been marked-I think eminently marked-by the avoidance of all semblance of party struggle, or the desire for party advantage. It is right that it should be so. No greater proiblem has ever confronted the people of Canada, and it is doubtful whether any problem, at any rate in our generation, will summon the people of Canada to share a greater burden, or call upon them for greater ico-operation in thought and in action, than this railway problem which faces us at this time. We can do no possible good by delving into the past and suggesting that it was not quite wise to have constructed large stretches of these railways when they were built and with the assistance which they received. All the talking that we can indulge in here will not turn back one page of history, or put back into the public exchequer one dollar that has already gone.
It is no use discussing the question that has been quite largely debated in this House as to whether government operation or private operation is the better. Nothing that we can do at present, so far as I can see, can take from the representatives of this country the Obligation to make the best they can of these roads. We have public ownership. There are some in this Chamber who, like mysellf, despite the majority of voices we have heard in debate, do not believe that public ownership is accompanied by the same economy or the same efficiency as private ownership. I have seen too much of the waste that is incidental to public management to be easily converted, even by a round of speeches, to a belief in the absolute efficiency and economy of public management. There is, I grant, a wave on in Canada, and perhaps all over the continent, at the present time in favour of public administration. It. may be the best thing for our country, but I do not subscribe to the belief that it is the cheapest, the most economical, or necessarily the most efficient system and there is an underlying reason. The private road, or the private utility, or the private company, hires whom it pleases and fires whom it pleases, and does not have to respond to the political dictation of the people whom it employs; and until you can write that out of public ownership you cannot have public ownership as independent and as efficient as private ownership. I do not suppose that I am in very much accord in that belief with many of the members of the group of this House of which I am a member; I do not suppose I am in accord with a single

gentleman who sits to the left of this group; I know I am in accord with some of the gentlemen who sit across the Chamber but not all of them. But it is not necessary, it is not worth while, to pursue this subject because we have public ownership and we are bound to make the best of it; and whether I believe it is the best thing or not it is my duty, if 'I Can help in any way to make that public ownership more popular or make it more efficient, to contribute what I can to that end. Perhaps nothing that I can contribute will be of value; but I have one thought in my mind Which I wish to express before the debate terminates.
You will pardon me a moment longer, Mr. Chairman, but I want to touch as lightly as I may upon some phases of the discussion, and to ask hon. members to consider how they may appear to the country and how they may appear to other members. We have heard-oh, I will not say much-but we have heard some reference in this House to all private enterprises as if there could not he such a thing as a private company unless it was accompanied by stock gambling, stock watering, graft and mismanagement. Now, as a citizen of Canada, I must say that I do not think that is a fair description of the bulk of our industrial enterprises; I would be very sorry to think so. I do think that the attacks largely come from an unconsidered habit of dealing with questions of this character by which people, more for the sake of oratory and more for the sake of inflaming the public mind, launch into a generalized attack upon every form of capital in the country; and I tell you it is absolutely unwise. In the year when we have to carry a debt as great as we are carrying, when we have to face the making up of a deficit as great as the deficit is, and must be on these railways, what we want to create in this country is confidence in its institutions, confidence in the capacity of this Parliament to find a solution of the problem, and confidence in the great industrial enterprises of Canada to see and to fight their way through this difficult period.
It is not the man who indulges in idle and ill-considered criticism who helps to build up the country. I am not an advocate of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I hold no brief for that organization. I do not think I ever received a dollar from them in my life. I do not expect and do not look for it, but in the part of Canada from which I come there is some apprecia-

Supply-Railways
tion of the great value to Canada of the development of that enterprise which has put Canada on the map of the world. I understand-and I think I am not wrong -that the Canadian Pacific has not been a company of watered stock. It got help, and not large help as we have measured later day subsidies, to put the line of steel across the continent; and in spite of much discouragement and many difficulties it did it. The Canadian Pacific Railway was the work of great master builders of empires, ruthless, possibly, at times, but valiant men, who saw their work and carried it through courageously. It is a work of which Canada may be proud. I know that in the East it does, at least, help one part of Canada, and help it magnificently, by simply doing the work for which it was created, and keeping the Canadian trade within Canadian channels. We can thank that railway for building up, at least, one of the ports within Canada, a doctrine which does not seem to have found very ready acceptance by some hon. members within the Chamber this session, but which I believe, after all, is the real aim of true Canadians who have vision enough to frame a policy for the whole of Canada and not for a section.
I trust that in whatever the minister does there will be no divorce, either by the Senate or by the House of Commons, of the Intercolonial Railway from the whole system of Government railways. Some people may take a partial view of it. The real future of the east is not in separation, but in greater and closer union. The same thing is true of the rest of Canada, and I hope that fact will be realized throughout Canada from end to end. Do not cut us off from the general system. We in the maritime provinces, in Halifax and St. John, give you your winter ports. You can find your summer ports on the Atlantic borders of this country as well. Keep us united with the railway system. Have the whole thing managed by the best brains that can be obtained, but let it be managed as a unit, and not as several distinct organizations, which will or may injure one another. At the same time give us a fair, reasonable and proper share of home rule. Let us have the administration within regions, by which the people in those regions can get more closely in contact with those who can feel the pulse of the business in the community, and shape the" course of the railway, so as to bring about the best development in each locality. I am not asking more special privileges but simply what every man asks
for, the opportunity of being easily heard, and of having just claims considered without delay, and without too much distance intervening. It was the policy of the late government to have-I will not say insisted-suggested or supported the idea that I believe took shape with the board of management of the railways to divide these railways into groups, or regional sections, where there would be an authority subject to the centre, and yet each authority would be supreme within the region. I believe, from remarks which have been made, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) does not intend to depart from that principle. I trust he will not, and in the constituency where my hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Copp) finds a very powerful vote in his support, I think the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) may advise that the centre of a very great region may be located.
I listened with great attention and much pleasure to the discussion of this matter by the hon. member from Marquette (Mr. Crerar). To my mind, he advanced principally two matters for consideration. First he was in agreement with us in the maritime provinces as to the question of regional administration, but he advanced another proposition. He thought that writing off charges against the railway, the funded debt, would give some assistance. I entirely concur with the statement of the hon. member from Brome (Mr. McMaster) that that is simply a question of book-keeping and does not touch the crux of the matter at all. We could get no possible relief from that. I am heartily in accord with my hon. friend from Marquette, when he suggests the colonization of this country along the line of railway. That is a good idea and I trust the Government will make every effort to give us colonization with the right kind of people.
I need not dilate further upon that matter, but I would like to remark that down to the present hour, with the exception of something that -fcras stated a few minutes ago, by, I think, the hon. member from Saskatoon (Mr. Evans) there has not been a hint, a whisper or a suggestion of anything that may be done to ease this problem, or to cut down the tens of millions of dollars of annual deficit. This is not a case where, by merely looking for some petty economy in the running of a private car or something of that kind, we are going to solve the problem. We have to go into bigger matters than that, and I think the member for Saskatoon came pretty near
Supply-Railways

the idea which I had in mind. Perhaps the idea is worth nothing, but I have confidence that, at least, there is the germ of a policy in it, and, therefore, I desire to present it to the House to-night.
In thinking over the problem I have been much impressed by a remark that was made, either by a gentleman in authority on the National Railways or someone on his behalf, perhaps a year ago, to the effect that the government railways were getting in a position to give the Canadian Pacific Railway a little healthy competition. I can understand a great many people in Canada applauding that remark, and thinking that a new and bright era was going to dawn for Canada, or their particular part of Canada, but, unfortunately, I do not construe that remark in that way. What does a little healthy competition mean when you get down to actual work and to dollars and cents? Commercial competition is commercial war, and commercial war is just as destructive of capital and resources as a war between nations. It may be less destructive in degree, but it is in the same character. What we want is not, I submit, the rivalry of two systems, each fighting the other, each trying to undercut and dislodge the other. What we want is harmonious cooperation between the two great systems for the purpose of giving the people, not the service that the people want-I am not going to use that phrase; I will be a little more careful of my language because I want to speak with a sense of responsibility-not the service the people want, but the service that this country can afford to give them, and that the people can pay for, not a service represented by a deficit, but a service which will produce a return sufficient to meet its cost. You cannot violate that principle without making the condition worse. What do we have? The hon. member for Saskatoon referred to parallelling conditions in the west and he spoke with knowledge and authority. I cannot follow him as to the geography of those roads; but I can invite the attention of this committee to something that, to my mind, is typical of general conditions and will illustrate the idea that I desire to submit for the consideration, not only of the minister, but of the committee as a whole. Travel, if you will, from Ottawa to Montreal; you can do it [DOT]by three separate lines.
Four.

Four if you like. These lines, I will grant you, serve different terri-

tory. Two of them are Canadian Pacific lines, one is a Grand Trunk line, and the other a Canadian National. The Canadian Pacific line that terminates in Place Viger station does not provide a rapid train; the Canadian National provides a train that might be classed as fairly rapid, a good through train with all the appointments; the Canadian Pacific short line does the same, and the Grand Trunk does the same.
I shall not advocate that anybody living on those routes shall be cut off from the world by the stopping of an entire line of railway; but I say that, if there were just plain, ordinary horse sense in the management of this business, the heads of the Canadian Pacific and the heads of the Canadian National would have talked together and would have arranged for one fast train to bring people who are in a hurry from Montreal to Ottawa or to take them back, instead of triplicating the fast trains. Accommodation trains would be run for the slower local service on each road, because you cannot get away from that without abandoning a road. That is only typical of conditions prevailing in many parts of the country. Hon. members will, perhaps, appreciate why I have asked this committee not to adopt the rather haughty language that impeaches the Canadian Pacific as if that company were a criminal standing at the bar of this House. That, in my judgment, is not the proper attitude to take.
In the army they have what is called a liaison officer, and what we want is something like a liaison committee. The Canadian Pacific will appoint from its directorate or its passenger or freight traffic experts a few men; the Canadian National will do the same, so that they will have equal numbers on such a committee or board or whatever you like to call it. They will bring expert knowledge to bear; they will confer about just such things as I am speaking of in relation to passenger business, and about things that I know nothing of in relation to freight business. The problem will be to advise each railway what can be cut out, what expense can be reduced and how much useful service can still be given to the public without duplication. I think that is the right spirit in which we should proceed. I admit I am not making a suggestion that is going to wipe out the deficit or anything of that kind; but having the idea that co-operation, ordinary conversation, ordinary meeting together to discuss these matters would be of value, I thought I would

take the opportunity of suggesting it to the minister and to the committee on this occasion as one slight contribution towards solving the railway problem.
Other hon. members may have better and more potent ideas than mine; but let us not rehash the question how this difficulty came about; let us make suggestions that will be helpful for the board, and that will cut down to some extent the tens of millions of dollars that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has to find, not for stock-watering, not for capitalists, but to provide for the people of Canada a service at just that much less than cost. If hon. members will visualise the matter in this way; if this country has to raise forty orfifty million dollars to pay the deficit, that money is not going to some bloated bondholder; it is going to give people freight rates lower than they ought to have, passenger rates lower than they ought to have. Until you face the problem in that way and also face the cost of providing the service-I say this in the widest sense-cut where cutting can be done, and get the people paying the cost of the service, a certain class of people are taking something out of the country every year instead of putting something into its exchequer. I cannot see the problem in any other way. The question is a simple one of arithmetic; it is also a question of principle. It is a question of policy, not great policy, not great strategy; it is simply the old homely idea of a man keeping within his income and, if he cannot do that, of finding means by which he will work harder and increase his income so as to catch up with the expenditures which he thinks are necessary.

We have had two days of very useful and instructive debate, and as regards the Government and the Minister of Railways, I am sure the ideas that have been expressed will all be given due consideration. The fact, however, remains that we have not as yet passed a single item. We have three items, one after the other, that all practically pertain to the matter under discussion. The suggestion which I would make to the committee is that we pass these items and then go on to the next; and at any time while the debate is in progress, or the committee is sitting on the estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals, members of the committee will have an opportunity of discussing the matter again if they see fit.

Those are
the items under which the general discussion of the question most properly comes, and as many members are absent from the House to-night, I should like to have the assurance' of the minister that, upon the other items in the estimates, a general discussion of the railway question will be permitted. If that is done, I see no objection upon our part to the three items going through. I understand that the two items that follow this and that provide for the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, have been passed upon by the board and have been approved. In view of that, I have no objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am at a loss for details because my deputy is not here, but in short I understand that it will mean doing away with the boys' camps this summer. I think the boys will bear with me for this season and shoulder their share of the sacrifice we are making in these estimates. The other boys' training can go on in the institutions as formerly, but there will not be any oamps this summer. I want to tell the committee that I am doing that for this year, and that is as far as any pledges will go, because if

the public understood this work, I am sure they would appreciate its great value. The number of cadets is increasing very greatly every year. This year we have a great many more than were ever enrolled before. To give the committee an idea of the work that is being done, I may say that the cadet training is carried out during the whole school year and includes instruction in signalling, first aid to the injured, physical exercise, organized games, elementary military drill, scouting and rifle shooting. Last year the cadet camps were of six days' duration, advance instruction being given in all the subjects I have enumerated. To show how the work is expanding I will read the following statement:

I regret very much to hear of the action the minister has taken with respect to the cadets. I think it is the blackest eye the militia of Canada has ever received to cut out the cadet camps held at Niagara, Barriefield, London and other places. The cadets were brought to these camps from the public, separate and the high schools all over the province and received a good training there. I do not know of any money appropriated by Parliament which has been spent to better advantage by the government than the money spent on the cadet service. The training the boys receive at these camps, instils patriotism into them; it is an education in itself, and furthermore I look on it as a work of religion. These children, after spending ten months of the year in their schools, are brought to the camps and remain there for a week or ten days. During that time they are given physical drill, camp life and a little military drill. They are also taught to be men, and they learn patriotism.
I look upon this item, out of the whole of the militia estimates, as one which should never have been interfered with. If there was one item which should have been left untouched by the Government it is the vote for the cadet service because the cadets to-day are the backbone of our militia. A cadet of fifteen or sixteen today is the volunteer later; nobody knows that better than the officers of our militia battalions. I saw the twelfth York battalion enter camp, along with others last summer, and many were cadets of seventeen and eighteen years of age. You are going to disorganize the whole militia if you wipe out this item. You are going in opposition to the popular demand, because there is a demand for cadet camps in Canj ada.
An organization has been formed in the city of Toronto (palled the Sportsmen's Patriotic Association and the Ontario Athletic Commission and it has already spent a great deal of money, preparing pupils of the public, separate and high schools for these camps this summer. The president is Mr. P. J. Mulqueen who is giving his services for nothing. Camps were to be held at Niagara, Barriefield, London other places. They have been preparing all winter for these camps where training will be given which will make good citizens of the boys of Ontario. The Association pro-* vide instructors who visit the public, separate and high schools one day a week during the winter months and teach the boys physical drill and games and give them other training and when the summer comes they will be ready to go to the cadet camps.
This is not militarism at all; it is building up Canadian youth. We are spending immense sums to aid the live stock industry. The city of Toronto itself has erected a building with this object in view at the cost of a million dollars. Such expenditures as these are all right in their way;^ but my complaint is that not enough iS being done by the Militia Department re cadet camps or by the Department of Health to develop the rising generation. The boy of to-day is the citizen of to-morrow. I am sorry that this Parliament is not spending even a five cent piece for the development of our youth. It can vote millions for railways but for building up character in Canada we have not a cent. The time is close at hand when the children from these schools should be aided to take the training I have mentioned, but how is it to be carried out if this vote is cut or disappears altogether? When I was at the Niagara camp last year I saw from seven to nine thousand children of all denominations, many of whom had come from the poorest slums of the cities and towns. Some of them were underfed. They went over on the Cayuga, the Corona, and other boats; and one boat came from Hamilton, General Mewburn's constituency.
Supply-Militia

The training the children receive at camps like that is of great advantage to them, and I am sorry to hear the minister get up at this late date and again change his estimates. If there is one minister whose estimates I would like to see go through more quickly than those of any other member of the Government it is the Minister of Militia. I have known him all my life; he is a good sportsman. The other day he came down and changed his estimates with respect to other services; and now he wants to make more changes and to cut out the vote for the cadet service. A night or two ago a sum of $25,000 was voted in aid of the Boy Scouts. It was money well spent; but I would like to see the minister do something for these cadet camps. If the work of these camps is stopped it will mean that the rising generation who come from places where the conditions are not good for physical development will suffer and have no recreation. Look at what has been done by the federal authorities in Washington, and by many of the state governments; they have multiplied by four or five their votes for the cadet services. In the parliament of the Australian Commonwealth an increased appropriation was introduced to provide for physical drill for the children, which the Minister of Defence declared he would never consent to cut off.
All this talk about militarism in this connection is futile. Not five per cent of the time in camp has been spent on military drill; games and physical recreation and sports of various kinds have been indulged in and the lads taught how to obey orders. I think that is something that is needed these days. The city from which I came is spending $11,000,000 in education this year, not omitting physical training. In the University of Toronto they are going to insist on physical drill. I hope the vote for this purpose will not be reduced or cut down. If it is it will mean that not only boys in Toronto, but boys in Aurora and other Ontario towns, will not be able to get to Niagara camp; the farm lads will suffer as well as. the city children. Why, children attended the Niagara camp from such long distances as New Ontario. One company of fifty boys came from Copper Cliff; they had never been much out of their own town before. At Niagara they mixed with boys from old Ontario, with mutually advantageous results. The education they receive there is worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to the government. I hope the

minister will re-consider his decision to reduce this vote. You cannot provide meals in camp for forty cents; at Niagara camp it costs sixty cents to properly feed the children. There are many other expenditures I would prefer to see reduced, or cut off altogether rather than the expenditure for this purpose which is going to build up character and stimulate patriotism in the children of Canada.
Many of the children who attend the Niagara camp are the sons of returned veterans. These men cannot afford to send their sons to play in the country and this camp has been a blessing to them. It has 'been a blessing to St. Catharines, Aurora, Newmarket, Copper Cliff and all the other cities and towns. I have letters from people in those districts asking me to do what I could. I urge the government to reconsider this item and give the public and separate school children a chance. Little enough money is being spent on the children. A dollar spent on the children will save later thousands of dollars in doctor bills, houses of correction, gaol farms and other institutions. By saving the rising generation and making good citizens of them, we are doing a great deal for the country. This is not a military work which the Militia Department has been doing; I look on it as a matter of religion. I hope the minister will reconsider the item. He has been a good friend of the Children. The cadets in Hamilton have been training for months and their teachers are working for nothing after -hours drilling them. The physical drill is far from military. Every university in Canada is going to insist on it. The largest universities in the States are insisting on physical exercises and participation in them by all the years in the university. The cadet movement is here to stay. This training is made compulsory in Australia and New Zealand. It is carried on in Great Britain, the United States and all over the world. I consider it one of the best works the government has undertaken.

I would like to join with the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) in urging anything that will extend physical training among the boys and girls of this Country. I also sympathize with any movement in the direction of giving an impetus to athletics, but I want to decidedly protest against any expenditure which will tend to develop the military spirit among the boys of this country, and this cadet training, though

Supply-Militia
it may be camouflaged1 as physical training, has as its object essentially the development of what has been called patriotism, but which, in the mouth of its exponents, is another word for militarism. I have before me a letter which was sent me by the mother of one of these boys who had been receiving this cadet training. He took his course during his high school work. The mother was under the impression that he was getting good physical training, that his character was being developed, and so on, but she learned immediately the boy was through his course that every effort was made to get him to join the local battalion. The letter reads:
Cambie St., Vancouver, B.C.
Dear Sir-I am writing you a personal appeal because I have watched with interest the cadet and physical training at the different schools in Vancouver.
You have now reached an age when you are to take your place as a citizen in this great new country of ours, of which there is none that can boast greater freedom or liberty for its citizens. As a unit in the British Empire it shares, not only the glories and liberties won in the past by our forefathers, but also shares in the glories of its history and its arms won in all countries of the globe, its literature and its commerce.
Have you ever stopped to think what you as a citizen will owe to this great country? You have been taught to sing "O, Canada," "The Maple Leaf," to swell with pride at tales of prowess, of the deeds of your forefathers, not only in the wars of Canada, but also in the wars in other parts of the world; of the part we played as Canadians in the Great War, and no doubt felt that, if need be, you would lay down your life for your country. But would not that be a silly sacrifice if in so doing you acomplished nothing. You know what happens to the boxer who goes into the ring without training; to the boy who, however plucky he may be, does not know how to defend himself. It is the same with nations; if one nation is indolent in preparing for its defence, and if it possesses, something that other nations covet, sooner or later it will have to defend its possessions. The surest way to prevent war is to be prepared for war.
The circular winds up by urging that this boy and others should arrange to join the 29th battalion of the 1st B.C. regiment. The letter is signed by H. S. Tobin, Lt. Col. Commanding 29th (Vancouver) Battalion, 1st B. C. Regiment.
It becomes very apparent from such a letter as that, and from other activities which we know are going on, that there is a distinct inducement held out to these cadets to enter upon a military career. There is more than that on the part if the officers who are training them; there is a distinct effort to build up the military spirit. I can quite appreciate that these officers are honest in that effort. I think
that they quite believe that that is what should be done, in order to carry out the patriotism which we all owe to our country, but I submit, Mr. Chairman, that those of us who do not believe in that have a right to help decide what the policy of this country is going to be. If we decide on a military policy, undoubtedly it for the experts to determine how that can best be carried out, but we stand at the point where we must decide the fundamental questions as to what the policy of the country is really going to be. If it is true, as this military officer says, that the surest way to prevent war is to prepare for war, by all means let us go ahead and train our boys. Let us proceed to carry out this idea with all the military expenditure that we can possibly afford. But some of us challenge that statement and that policy. We were told some years ago that if we went into this last war it would be an end to all wars. I say that those who made that statement have absolutely deceived us; they have proved that they were false prophets and that they did not know what they were talking about. We listened to them and went into the war. Do we find that the war has ended wars? Now, we are told by some of the self-same gentlemen-at least by those who advocate the self-same policy- that we have to be prepared for an even greater European war than that through which we have just passed. We gave of our best, and I, for one, have every respect for the men who joined the colours, because they believed they were doing their duty. I think that when these men come back they should receive the very best this country has. We asked them to go and risk their lives, and many of them laid down their lives. Those that come back and the dependents of those who did not come back should receive the best. But that consideration does not make me believe that we should prepare to follow along lines of public policy which in the past have proved to be so disastrous. Never was there a better opportunity on such a world-wide scale for demonstrating the advantages of war; and never was there a greater failure in the history of the whole human race. If ever we had a demonstration of the futility of war we had it in this Great War. And now, notwithstanding that demonstration, we are trying to inculcate these self-same ideas of militarism in our children.
A little over a year ago the cadets of Vancouver city were reviewed in the King
Supply-Militia

Edward High School by a brigadier gen-' eral. In encouraging the boys, he referred to the splendid showing which they had made as a result of their training, and he made this statement: "That nation whose boys can think clearly and can shoot straight is the nation that will be able to impose its will on other nations." That teaching is what we have ordinarily termed Prussianism-Prussianism pure and simple, and Prussianism does not look any more attractive to me in a British uniform than it does in a German uniform. We have complained again and again that, during the last few decades, the Germans have inculcated this military spirit in the minds of their young people; that they have introduced this teaching into their colleges, and that the whole of Germany was simply permeated by the military spirit. I have seen myself, in some of the universities in Germany, the result of that spirit, where those young college fellows dared not refuse to accept a challenge to a duel, and I have watched these student duels, as with a great deal of nerve, each man makes a thrust at the other fellow, all this being done to encourage the military spirit. I remember one of these students saying to me some years ago: "Oh, you Britishers; you have lost your old military spirit, your old military prowess; away back in the time of Shakespeare, you were a nation with noble ideals; to-day you are a nation of shopkeepers; you have lost the military spirit." That was the German idea of the situation, but we sit here tonight and listen to an hon. gentleman rejoice in the fact that we, in this day, in our universities are adopting the policy that Germany adopted thirty or forty years ago. I do not decry physical training in our universities; I am glad of it. I do not decry athletics in our universities. A few years ago I rejoiced to take my share in the athletics of my university. We do not want however to introduce military training into our universities, and we do not want to militarise the Canadian people.
It has been said that we want our boys to grow up to be manly boys. I have a boy of fourteen years of age taking his training in the high school, and my boy to-day is% practically penalised because I refused to allow him to take cadet training. I did so, not because I did not want my boy to grow up to be strong, to participate in athletics and all the rest of it; but I refused absolutely to allow him to he placed under those conditions in which he would be likely 'o develop anything of a military spirit,
[Mr. Woodsworth.T
because I believe that militarism to-day is bankrupt and has demonstrated its bankruptcy. Somebody might say that this was merely a personal opinion of mine; but I want to repeat what I said here the other evening, that, in speaking along these lines, I am speaking, not merely for myself, but, I think, for a considerable group of the labour men whom I know very intimately from Fort William to the Pacific coast. I think I have a right to speak for a large number of labour people, as I have received again and again communications from all parts of this country endorsing this position. I have an undoubted right to speak for my own constituency where this was one of the questions that we took up very definitely in the election campaign, where I received the fullest endorsation with regard to my position on military training in the schools and where we have discussed out this question in our municipal as well as in the federal and provincial campaigns. Under such circumstances, we have a right, in the consideration of these items, to consider frankly whether or not we wish, in the future, to continue to carry out a policy which must lead us into the same troubles into which militarism has led the race from the earliest times which history records.
Some hon. members will say: "What else is there ahead"? I submit that we might very well make some peace expenditures that would do a great deal more good than these war expenditures. This is not the time to suggest these things to the House; but I for one believe that if this Parliament voted a few of the millions that it is spending on military estimates, to feed the starving children of Russia, it would be an expenditure which would go a long way to cement international friendship. Other things that we could do could readily be mentioned. Why should we constantly think there is no other way in which we can spend our money for defence purposes than by maintaining a military force? We shall have a cessation of wars so soon as we remove the economic causes which are producing wars, and as soon as we remove those other causes which prejudice one nation against another. I should like to express in this House the hope-again if you like since other opinions have been expressed here again and again-that we, in this young Canada of ours where we have no enemy at our gates, would take the lead in working out some of these principles of good fellowship. I for one rejoice because of having come of parents and

Supply-Militia
grandparents who have been born in Canada, and this is my idea of patriotism. I think we are able to take the lead because of our connection with the great British Empire. I for one do not want to avoid any obligation that arises because of our connection with the British Empire; but we can fulfil our obligations in other than military fashion. There is, on the one hand, the tie that we have with Great Britain, and, on the other, the close connection that we have with the people of the United States to the south of us. We stand, it seems to me, in a unique position to foster those newer ideals, in which alone we believe the safety of the world consists. Within the last few days, it has been stated on the floor of this House that troubles are looming up in Europe to-day. Are we going to be drawn into this maelstrom of European troubles? Rather than that, I would say that we Canadians would have to stand here if needs be by ourselves to uphold the principles of peace. America has been separated more or less by the oceans from the old world. In the last few years we have seen the suicidal policies of Europe. Unless we are careful, those yellow races about which we talked a few days ago, are going to witness, as one of the great Counts of Japan said, the suicide of European peoples and the end of European civilization.
Carried.

Yes, carried, if you like. I have just about finished my remarks. I will vote for the amendment because it is a little better than the original estimate. We believe in taking small mercies. These things that I have been saying are things that, whether we like to hear them in this House or not, are things that are being talked and thought about by the ordinary people of this country from one coast to the other, and we in this House would be well advised if we endeavoured to keep a little more closely in touch with the current thought of the common people who suffered most in the last war.

I do not want to delay the passage of this item, but I desire to add my protest to that of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) against the suggestion that this vote for cadet purposes should be reduced by the substantial sum of $100,000. We are, of course, all aware that the minister has committed himself, since he brought his estimates to Parliament, to a substantial all-round reduction.
All I propose to do is to protest against the reduction of this item. As I read down the estimates of the Militia Department I see several places where reductions might possibly be made which would cause less inconvenience and loss to the militia of Canada than would the reduction which is now proposed in regard to the cadet service in this country.

What items do you refer
to?

Wait until we come to them; I will explain then. The cadet service has not heretofore been looked upon as purely military service at all. It has been considered in this country, and I think in other countries as well, more in the nature of athletic development than as military training; and I am sure that in the future, as in the past, the Government will continue the service with that end in view.
Why not buy some hockey sticks?

This training has been regarded as the very best athletic development, being given under a system of military discipline. Military discipline and military training lend themselves with great advantage to physical development, and the best physical development that is given, whether in boys' or girls' schools, follows generally along the lines of military training. But that does not make it military training at all; it still retains the essence of physical development. And physical training is what is chiefly sought by the vote now under consideration. The expenditure is not a large one. Indeed, $450,000 for the development of the young men of this country is a very infinitesimal sum. Could we employ the money better in any other avenue of expenditure which we have in the Dominion at the present time? Last year's estimate of $450,000 provided for an annual camp for 8,000 cadets. That camp, it was estimated, would cost about $125,000. I assume that the estimate, when first brought down to Parliament at $450,000 all told, had in view the expenditure of about $125,000 on this annual training which is given to the boys in Canada. Now, it certainly is a splendid outing for them; it is a good holiday; it is a camp under strict supervision, where not only the physical condition of the boys, but their moral welfare as well is looked after. The moral conditions and the living conditions generally that obtain in these camps are of the highest standard. That $125,000 is money

as well spent as any we have expended in the Dominion, and I think that the minister should strain a point to rearrange these reductions, if he is bound to reduce, so that $125,000 may he spent on the boys in the annual summer camps. I think the camps are now held pretty generally throughout Canada. At all events, they were last year. It is not a movement confined to one province; it is now developed in all provinces, I believe, and it is growing with great rapidity. It is supported, I think, by the best elements in the community, by the best educationalists in Canada, by the various churches, without regard to denomination; and it is endorsed by leading medical and commercial men, as well as by agricultural people throughout
