He can do a greater service by allowing these boys to go through the annual camp than by cutting this item by $100,000 as proposed. I do not want to delay the item at all; I want the House to deal with it as speedily as possible. But I certainly want to make my protest and to suggest that the minister recast his estimates and save the situation.

There is one point I
want to make clear. My hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) seems to convey the impression that he represents Labour. I might say that when I was nominated the Labour candidate did me the honour to withdraw, and I got 95 per cent of the Labour vote in the district I represent. I have always supported the cadet movement and the militia, and will continue to do so. In fact, I should consider myself a traitor to the people I represent if I did not, and I am sorry to see this amount cut down. These boys should get the training to which they are justly entitled. I regret also that the militia training item is reduced, and I am more than sorry that there is not more money in the estimate for the navy. I do not believe in training our young people for the purpose of offensive, but I do believe in training them so that they may be able to defend themselves if ever the time comes they are called upon to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is no better friend to the cadet movement in Canada than I, myself. I have always been their friend, as a private citizen as well as throughout my public career. But we are asking the militia and everybody else this year to

make some sacrifice, and I do not believe that the boys will be any the worse off for feeling that they too are doing their share. One year is as far as I can make any pledge, because I fully agree that the training of the cadets, apart from any military idea at all, lays the foundation for the physical and mental manhood of the Dominion. The only thing that will be reduced is the expenditure in connection with the annual camps. The other training the boys receive in the collegiate institutes, in the public schools, in the high schools and in the universities will be carried on as usual.

I was greatly pleased to hear the minister speak so highly of this branch of the serviee. He is conversant with what is done in his own town, and I know something about the matter myself. I believe that cadet training is one of the most valuable services we can render the youth of the country. Has the minister considered the possible very serious effect, upon all the training throughout the rest of the year, of the knowledge of these boys that they cannot look forward to the outing which the camp usually affords them? I am afraid it will tend to demoralize their training throughout the rest of the year.

speechtext: I shall have to correct my hon. friend. The annual training of the militia is not to be dispensed with, but only slightly reduced.

the navy is also reduced, if the minister has his way. In fact, it would appear that everything in the nature of national defence is to be materially reduced, if not entirely dispensed with. speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Which he did not do.

I could not help but think, as I listened to the arguments which were advanced, of the example we shall be setting to the youth of this country. Instead of cultivating and developing a vigorous spirit among the youth, of our country, what sort of a spirit are you likely to develop by cutting down these essential features of national defence? I notice an increase of $35,000 in this particular item. The Government are bound to reduce, so that they will be ineffective for any useful purpose, the items for important and essential features of national defence, while the non-essential items are being increased. The reductions that are being made in the essential features of national defence are such as to cripple the service and make it absolutely useless. I do not expect the Government will take any notice of any protest which may be lodged, but as a citizen of this country, as a representative of the people, and as the father of growing boys in this country, I refuse to
countenance any such policy as this. I have altogether too much respect for the traditions of our country especially in this age, after such a splendid example having been set to the people of the world by those who participated in the late war to have any sympathy at all with those who would claim that now it is the duty of Canada to blaze the way, as it were, for the rest of the world in becoming a spineless people who will stand for anything rather than defend ourselves against any emergency which may develop in the future.
That is the policy which is to-day being [DOT]advocated by the Government of this country. The minister to-night, after bringing down his estimates, calmly gets up and informs the House that he cannot move to reduce the items, so his colleague sitting next to him gets up and moves to reduce *item after item that would serve a useful purpose, but when it comes to the nonessential items, such as the one now before us they are being increased. There is no move on the part of his colleague to reduce tfiis item.
Why is it that the non-essentials are being maintained, and even increased, while the essentials are being so absolutely impaired as to be of no effective service whatever? Some hon. members may say "Oh, but see the time we are taking up in discussing these estimates." I suppose as time passes a feeling of apathy will come over the House and the remark will be made "What is the use of this anyway"? As one member of Parliament, I absolutely refuse to countenance any such policy as is recommended here; and I say-and I am most emphatic in my view-that the day is not far distant when the policy the Government is now advocating will be conclusively shown to be just as foolish and just as shortsighted as the policy which was advocated early in 1914, when we were on the verge of the Great War.
I was somewhat amazed to hear the terms in which the Prime Minister referred to the policy of the party of which he was a member at that time. I could not help but recall, as he was arguing that the policy his party advocated was the right one, a statement made by the late Colonel Roosevelt in 1917 when he said: "The only reason the war has not been brought to this country is because of Britain's navy and the British and French armies." The policy of this Government undoubtedly is "Somebody will take care of us; it won't be necessary for us to make any sacrifices in the event of any trouble arising. We have

the British navy back of us and after all nothing may happen."
But there is a duty imposed upon every citizen of Canada. His first duty is to see that he maintains, and perpetuates to the utmost of his power, and bequeaths to his children unsullied, the heritage which has been handed down to him-a heritage secured at great sacrifice by those who have gone before. We cannot afford to place that heritage in jeopardy because of the fact that it might cost something to maintain it. This is the first duty of our citizens, but it is a duty which this new Government has lost sight of. I am afraid the Government is attempting to carry out some promises made before the election by the policy it is now advocating. I protest as vigorously as I can against what has already been done and what is proposed to oe done.
I am surprised that the member of the Government who is now sitting to the right of the Minister of Militia is not, if he intends to be consistent, attempting to reduce this item in some way, because he has cleanly indicated to the House that the Government proposes to dispose of these properties. He has intimated that negotiations are on foot to dispose of the arsenal at Lindsay and this is not a good time to sell some of these properties. Why were these properties purchased? What use have they been put to in the past? Will the ,minister now tell us what properties the Government is negotiating to dispose of in addition to the arsenal at Lindsay? Will he tell us what the arsenal at Lindsay has cost. The minister is also going to dispose of, or disperse, the navy; the submarines are going to be sunk, they are not going to be put into use at all; and he is going to maintain an arsenal down on the St. Lawrence. Why, if he does that, in the event of trouble occurring, a submarine may come up the St. Lawrence some night and blow the whole thing up. If there is one place where there should not be an arsenal it is the city of Quebec. The policy of the Government is to place in jeopardy the very establishment needed for the manufacture of ammunition in this country. I ask the committee to consider well what it is doing. I must say that I am surprised that the Minister of Militia, whom I have known for many years, would be a party to such proceedings, that he would allow himself to be made the mouthpiece of a party that is endeavouring to put into effect in Canada any such policy as this.

I desire to call attention to the significant silence of certain members who sit on this committee now and who sat here a year ago when these matters were under discussion. The hon. member from Quebec South (Mr. Power) was in the House until a few minutes ago. He has now left the Chamber, and I call

the attention of the House to the fact that when this item was under discussion a year ago the amount which was asked in the estimates was six and a half millions, the hon. member from Quebec South moved that it be reduced by two million dollars, and every hon. member who then sat on this side of the House, in opposition, voted for that reduction. I think my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) was one of them-I am sure he was. The silence of these hon. members on this occasion rather staggers me. I thought they were serious. From their remarks last year one would judge they were serious. But a year has passed and the vote to-day standing at five and a half million is practically going unchallenged by those hon. members who moved last year for a reduction of $2,000,000. I certainly am not going to move for a reduction of the item. I believe it is just and proper and should be retained. What think you, Mr. Chairman, of 30 or 40 hon. members of this House who sat in opposition last year, and solemnly voted to reduce the item by $2,000,000, who have not the courage on the present occasion to move to reduce the item by a single cent?

I do not wish to let the remarks of the hon. member from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) go unchallenged. So much has been said that I desire to say that I, as one from the province of Ontario, appreciate the action of the minister in starting off in the right direction in endeavouring to reduce the expenditure of the Dominion of Canada at the present time. That is one thing which we all want. I was in this House, and I may have supported a reduction of $2,000,000 in this estimate last year. I could not say whether I did or not, as I have not the estimate before me. The minister has already reduced this item by $755,000, thus showing that he is starting in the right direction, and as is said, "Well begun is half done." But since the militia estimates and other estimates too have been brought down in this House, we have witnessed something that, to my knowledge, has not happened in the House of Commons in the Dominion of Canada since confederation, and that is the Government desiring to reduce expenditure and the Opposition emphatically pounding and abusing the Government for doing so. At this time, I think the people of this Dominion are looking to the Government to reduce expenditures as much as possible under present conditions, and they will appreciate any reductions. I am of opinion also that the same feeling would have pre-

vailed throughout the country had the Conservative party been in power.
We have heard a good deal about the cadets not getting their drill; but in Canada there are other boys than those whom we want to train as boy scouts and cadets, boys whom we want to train up to be good citizens of this country. Only to-day I received a letter from a man whose only son and support went overseas and made the supreme sacrifice. This man, who is over sixty years of age, is, through misfortune, unable to earn his living, and to-day he is without his only son whom he raised and upon whom he depended for support. My room-mate, the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) is on the Pension Committee where such matters are being discussed, and I think we ought to be fair to the people who have made the supreme sacrifice and to their dependents before we start building up more militarism in this country.
Some people are not very consistent. We had the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) saying that, in his constituency, there was militia property that was growing up with weeds, and wanting to know what was going to be done with it, and then we had the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) finding fault with the Government for trying to do something with property that was not of use. Why not sell the property and turn the money into the treasury of the country, or give it to the dependents of those men who went overseas and made the supreme sacrifice instead of using this money to send our young men to the camps to be trained for militarism?
A day or so ago I had a letter in regard to the family of a man who enlisted, but who did not get overseas. This man was in a camp training, and owing to the effects of an electrical storm he died, leaving a widow with nine of a family dependent upon her. According to the law, the Pension Committee cannot give anything to the widow. If this property is of no use, why not sell it and give the money to those people to help them out? I am in favour of making any reduction possible, not only in this estimate, but in other estimates as well. I am not against the militia of this country, but if we can save a little on the estimates this year, it is our duty and the duty of the Government to be faithful to the people who sent us here and to reduce the estimates if we possibly can.

If the House wishes me to move a reduction in the face of those protests, I am willing to do so; but unless the House wishes that, I would rather not. If hon. gentlemen from all groups could know the protests that I have received from all quarters, I think they would say that I have acted wisely in not making this reduction. I think I should make this explanation to the committee.
It would be well for us to get this item through as quickly as possible. Otherwise, we may have some more changes before the item carries.

Item agreed to.
Schools of instruction, $140,000.
I move in amendment that this item be reduced by an amount of $50,000.
I should like to have some information with regard to the instruction that is given.
And where these schools are.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is a School of Military Engineering at Chatham; gunnery staff course; ordnance officers' course; Artillery College, Woolwich; officers' class in artillery college; inspection of ordnance machinery; master gunners' course at Woolwich; armament artificers' course, Woolwich; laboratory course, etc. I have a long list.
Item as amended agreed to.
Topographic Survey, $45,000.
I am informed that this is one item in the militia estimates that might very well be cut out for one year at least. What explanation has the minister in regard to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The following is the statement which has been prepared by the officers of the department:
Particulars of Topographic Survey referred to under "General Purpose", page 1.
Established in 1902 on the advice of the Imperial Authorities for the purpose of producing reliable topographic maps of Canada, primarily for military purposes, but also sold to the public, who appreciate them for various civil uses. With the exception of isolated areas mapped by the Geological Survey, these are the only topographic maps produced in Canada. Up to 1913 the completed drawings of the map sheets were sent to the War Office for reproduction and printing, but this plan was found unsuitable and a complete photo litho printing plant was established at Ottawa as part of the Survey division, and has been operating successfully from 1914 to date, printing all maps and diagrams required. The Survey division is thus enabled to do all the work involved in producing first Class maps, from the initial survey to printing the map.
Besides the regular series of 1" and i" maps a large number of other maps and diagrams have been produced,-larger scale maps of camp areas, various maps, diagrams, lantern plates, etc., for the use of trootps in training, schools of instruction, Royal Military College, etc. Original plates of all maps, etc. are preserved and reprints made as required.
The 1" maps show all water features, boundaries and nature of timber. County, township and city boundaries, concessions and lots are indicated. All public roads, railways, bridges, settlements, factories, forges and houses (wood or stone) at time of survey. The relief of the
S n p ply-M ilitia

ground surface is shown by contours at 25 ft. vertical intervals and the eflevation at many road corners.
The area surveyed and mapped to date is shown on the attached index maps.
Sq. miles
Total area mapped	 32,000
Surveyed, not mapped	 5,500
Partly surveyed	 5,000
In addition to making surveys and printing maps as above, the Survey division acts as a School of Instruction in Surveying for N.C.O's and men of the Permanent Force, with the object of selecting the best men to fill vacancies in the staff of the Survey division as they occur, and also to provide a nucleus of trained men in the Permanent Force for a Field Survey section. Ten men are at present under instruction (since January 1st) at Ottawa in theoretical work. They will be attached to survey parties as assistants for the summer, for practical work in the field.
The total at present consists of twenty-nine, all technical men,-surveyors, topographers, lithographic map draughtsmen, map engraver, litho-photographer, lithographer and transferrer, litho-pninter, office clerks and two helpers. Twenty-one of the above are permanent divil servants, who are paid from civil government salaries.

I agree that this is one of the important votes in the militia estimates. It is not for the value of the map as a map. I believe that, at the rate they are going, the map will be completed in about two hundred years. There are portions of Canada already completed. These maps are very useful for automobilists, etc., as road maps, and a small amount is received by way of revenue by the Government through the sale of them. This is one of the most important parts of the military education. Map drafting and map reading are two very important elements in military instruction, and it is for that purpose that this vote is carried from year to year, far more than for the purpose of issuing a topographic map of Canada, important as that may be, if we can ever complete one. I was under the same impression as my hon. friend (Mr. Hanson) two or three years ago when I questioned the item, but General Sir Arthur Currie and Major General MacBrien explained fully to me the real object of the vote. It is to carry out the training of officers in order that they may instruct non-commissioned officers and men in the important subject of map drawing, and perhaps in the equally important subject of map reading. I do think, though, that the question of topographic surveys in this country is far too extended. I believe that in no fewer than four, and possibly five, departments we are making surveys and drafting maps, all of which should be done in the Department

of Militia, where there are trained engineers and officers, who are quite competent to do that work and are now under pay. The expense would be very greatly reduced if survey work and the drafting of maps, now done by different departments, were carried out by the officers of the Militia Department. I made this suggestion to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) when his estimates were going through, and I trust that some one department of government will take the matter up and consolidate those various activities.
Mr. GRAHAM. My hon. friend is right. That matter has been considered, and at present we have a committee of officers from the various departments to look into the question and see whether there is not some way by which the work can be concentrated in one department. Each department, I imagine, thinks it is best fitted to do the work, but I agree that the standard of map the Militia Department produces shows that that department has facilities equal to, if not better than, those of other departments.

The remarks of the
member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) would apply to geodetic surveys, but I cannot see any possible reason why the vote should be carried this year for topographic survey work. Map reading, from a topographic viewpoint, is easy; any schoolboy can do that. From the military viewpoint it is the geodetic map that is required.

Item agreed to.
Training areas, $15,000.

What is this amount
for?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have cut the item
in two this year. It is for the purpose of purchasing any right of way that juts into training areas. We have no expenditure in view, but if it should occur that a piece of land juts into a training area the vote is provided so that we may be able to purchase it. The probabilities are that not a dollar will be spent.

Item agreed to.
Transport and Freight, $200,000.

My remarks in regard
to other items apply to this one. This is a case where the works are gone but the overhead remains. If you are going to do away with a large percentage of military camps

Supply-Militia
what is the necessity for $200,000 for transport and freight? Surely the item can be cut down.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Last year the whole of
the vote was expended but $2,000.

But you are cutting
down your camps at least 30 per cent, and it stands to reason than an item of this kind should be reduced. I would suggest that the minister get busy now and make a substantial reduction.
I move that this item be reduced by $60,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of the committee to adopt the amendment.
Amendment negatived.
I move in amendment that the item be reduced by $10,000. That is the reduction the minister volunteered to make a few days ago.

When the estimates were before the House at an earlier stage I cited several items from the Auditor General's report. I referred particularly to an item with respect to transportation and travelling expenses of staff. A good deal of travelling was done by officers around Saskatchewan, as I pointed out before; and I mentioned certain items of theatre tickets and various other things which these officers evidently seemed to think the people of the country should pay for. In the vote for transport and freight, which includes these travelling expenses, no reduction is made from the amount voted last year. I used Military District No. 12 as an illustration; if the same conditions obtain in all the other districts in proportion to size, then a huge sum of money is wasted in that manner. If these officers believe they have the right to spend the people's money in this way, then it is our duty at this moment to reduce this vote by the amount which in our opinion, is being wasted in that manner. Now, there is an amendment before the committee-
Move another one.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It is moved by Mr. Spencer that vote No. 110, transport and freight, be reduced by the sum of $10,000. Is it the pleasure of the committee that the amendment carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

The vote for annual drill has been reduced by thirty per cent.
Is there any proportionate reduction of transport and freight?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This vote is for transportation and travelling expenses of officers of headquarters and district staff, officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the permanent and active militia on change of station or travelling on duty, except duties connected with annual drill, cadet services, etc. It has nothing to do with the annual drill. Last year the whole amount of the vote was expended within $2,000. I ask the committee to put the item through as it is; any amount that can be saved out of the appropriation surely will be. What effect it would have to reduce the item by $10,000 when it has not anything to do with the other reductions, I am not in a position to say at this moment.

I was rising to my feet when the hon. member got up who presented the resolution for a reduction of $50,000. I had in mind the soft impeachment of the hon. member for South Wellington and it was my intention to move in amendment that this vote be reduced by $25,000, an action which would be consistent with the statement I had previously made regarding these expenditures. I believe it would be well if it should be understood throughout the country that the people do not want these joy rides which go under the name of " staff rides "; at least, they do not want the excesses which these men indulge in when taking these staff rides. I believe the House would do well to give these gentlemen-gallant gentlemen, let us call them-a lesson by asking them to reduce their lavish expenditures by some $25,000, and I offer that as an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is already an amendment to reduce the item by $10,000. I think the item should not be reduced, for the reasons I have given. I thoroughly understand my hon. friend's impression with regard to certain things that took place; I have had some particulars in that regard brought to my mind during the last few days. But that is a very exceptional case, and I am sure it will not occur again. Money expended in that way is certainly not expended as, I presume, Parliament intended it should be. But I would ask the hon. member not to press his amendment, because I am not sure of what its effect would be on the work of the department. This was one of the amounts
Supply-Public Works

that was fully expended last year; it has reference to services not connected with others which have been reduced. I assure my hon. friend that the performance to which he has referred is not likely to occur again.

I am quite satisfied with the explanation of the hon. minister; I am sure he will look into these things and bring the matter to the notice of those who, we think, have erred.
Amendment (Mr. Spencer) negatived.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think we have done pretty good work. There is an item of war claims, but I would nor like to press it to-night. It is a very large vote, and I would also like to have the member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn) here when it is discussed. He is chairman of the War Graves Commission, which met recently and decided upon a course to be followed in the erection of memorial monuments. He is better posted on the details than anyone else, and I should like to have him here to explain what this commission is doing and what it proposes to do.
Progress reported.
